Bilinear formalism for Schwarzian KP
and Harry Dym hierarchies

V. Prokofev ††thanks: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology, 143026, Moscow, Russia and National Research University Higher School of Economics, 20 Myasnitskaya Ulitsa, Moscow 101000, Russia, e-mail: vadprokofev@gmail.com    A. Zabrodin ††thanks: National Research University Higher School of Economics, 20 Myasnitskaya Ulitsa, Moscow 101000, Russia; e-mail: zabrodin@itep.ru
April 2026

We consider the Schwarzian KP and Harry Dym hierarchies in the framework of the bilinear formalism which is well known for such integrable hierarchies as KP, modified KP, BKP, Toda lattice and other. We show that, similarly to the bilinear formulation of the modified KP hierarchy, the Schwarzian KP can be reformulated as an integral bilinear equation for a pair of KP tau-functions with the property that any linear combination of them is again a tau function of the KP hierarchy. The Harry Dym hierarchy is then obtained as the Lax-Sato formulation of the SchKP one. The close connection with Bäcklund-Darboux transformations for integrable hierarchies is also discussed. Besides, it is shown that the SchKP hierarchy has a natural embedding into the multi-component KP hierarchy.

1 Introduction

In this article, we revisit the Schwarzian KP (SchKP) and Harry Dym (HD) integrable hierarchies and suggest a formulation of them by means of the bilinear formalism. The main hero is the tau-function satisfying certain bilinear differential equations (or functional relations). In a nutshell, we deal with the three basic versions of the integrable KP hierarchy (KP, modified KP (mKP), SchKP) and trace the connections between them:

KP⟷modified KP⟷Schwarzian KP (Harry Dym).\mbox{KP}\longleftrightarrow\mbox{modified KP}\longleftrightarrow\mbox{Schwarzian KP (Harry Dym)}. (1.1)

For the KP and mKP hierarchies both bilinear and Lax-Sato formulations, as well as their equivalence, are well known. The bilinear formulation of the SchKP hierarchy seems to be new. In this approach, the HD hierarchy arises as the Lax-Sato reformulation of the SchKP one.

The Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation was suggested in 1970 [2, 3]. It has the form

3​uy​y=(4​ut−6​u​ux−ux​x​x)x.3u_{yy}=\Bigl(4u_{t}-6uu_{x}-u_{xxx}\Bigr)_{x}. (1.2)

This equation is the first member of an infinite hierarchy of integrable equations known as the KP hierarchy. The modern understanding of this hierarchy is based on the works of the Kyoto school [4, 5] (see also books [6, 7]), where the bilinear approach was developed and its equivalence to the Lax-Sato formulation was proved. The universal dependent variable is the tau-function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) depending on an infinite number of independent variables (“times” 𝐭={t1,t2,t3,…}{\bf t}=\{t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},\ldots\} with t1=xt_{1}=x, t2=yt_{2}=y, t3=tt_{3}=t) and satisfying an infinite number of bilinear differential equations. All of them are encoded in the following bilinear integral functional relation:

∮C∞eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(𝐭′+[z−1])​𝑑z=0,\oint_{C_{\infty}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}},z)}\,{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau({\bf t^{\prime}}+[z^{-1}])dz=0, (1.3)

which holds for all 𝐭{\bf t}, 𝐭′{\bf t}^{\prime}. Here the standard notations are used:

ξ⁡(𝐭,z)=∑k≥1tk​zk,𝐭±[z−1]={t1±z−1,12​z−2,13​z−3,…}.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\xi({\bf t},z)=\sum_{k\geq 1}t_{k}z^{k},}\\ \\ {\bf t}\pm[z^{-1}]=\Bigl\{t_{1}\pm z^{-1},\,\frac{1}{2}z^{-2},\,\frac{1}{3}z^{-3},\,\ldots\Bigr\}.\end{array} (1.4)

The contour C∞C_{\infty} is a big circle of radius R→∞R\to\infty. The function u=u⁡(x,y,t)u=u(x,y,t) in (1.2) is expressed through the tau-function as u=2​∂x2log⁡τu=2\partial_{x}^{2}\log\tau.

Later some other appearances of the KP equation and the KP hierarchy were suggested. The most widely known one is the modified KP (mKP) hierarchy. Its first member has the form

vx​x​x​x−4​vx​t+3​vy​y+6​vx​x​vy−6​vx2​vx​x=0.v_{xxxx}-4v_{xt}+3v_{yy}+6v_{xx}v_{y}-6v_{x}^{2}v_{xx}=0. (1.5)

In the literature there exist several different versions of the mKP hierarchy (see [8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14]). We will mostly deal with the Kupershmidt and Kiso version [8, 9, 10]. Its bilinear formulation requires two tau-functions τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}), τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) rather than one. Each of them is a KP tau-function (i.e., satisfies the integral bilinear equation (1.3)), and, in addition, there is a set of bilinear equations which link them together. The dependent variable v=v⁡(x,y,t)v=v(x,y,t) in (1.5) is v=log⁡(τ^/τ)v=\log(\hat{\tau}/\tau). The transition from τ\tau to τ^\hat{\tau} is an example of what is called (auto) Bäcklund-Darboux transformation for the KP hierarchy, i.e., a transformation that sends any solution to another solution. A more general point of view is based on the embedding of the mKP hierarchy into the more general 2D Toda lattice hierarchy [15]. In this approach, the tau-function τ⁡(n,𝐭)\tau(n,{\bf t}) depends also on a discrete variable n∈ℤn\in\mbox{\Bbb Z}, and one identifies τ⁡(𝐭)=τ⁡(n,𝐭)\tau({\bf t})=\tau(n,{\bf t}), τ^​(𝐭)=τ​(n+1,𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\tau(n+1,{\bf t}) for some fixed value of nn.

The Schwarzian KP equation first appeared in [16] in the context of Painlevé analysis as the singularity manifold equation associated with the KP equation. It has the form

(4​StSx−{S,x})x=3​(SySx)y+32​(Sy2Sx2)x.\left(4\frac{S_{t}}{S_{x}}-\{S,x\}\right)_{x}=3\left(\frac{S_{y}}{S_{x}}\right)_{y}+\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{S_{y}^{2}}{S_{x}^{2}}\right)_{x}. (1.6)

Here

{S,x}=Sx​x​xSx−32​(Sx​xSx)2\{S,x\}=\frac{S_{xxx}}{S_{x}}-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{x}}\right)^{2} (1.7)

is the Schwarzian derivative. Equation (1.6) is invariant under fractional-linear transformations of the variable S=S⁡(x,y,t)S=S(x,y,t). The corresponding SchKP hierarchy was discussed in [17, 18, 19, 20].

The original (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional version of the HD equation was suggested by Harry Dym in 1973–1974 in an unpublished paper. It is the following nonlinear partial differential equation for a function U⁡(s,t)U(s,t) of two variables s,ts,t:

4​Ut=U3​Us​s​s.4U_{t}=U^{3}U_{sss}. (1.8)

In the literature, this equation first appeared in 1975 in Kruskal’s paper [21], and received the name of its discoverer. A slightly different version of the HD equation arises in the the Saffman–Taylor problem with surface tension [22]. Later, in 1984, Konopelchenko and Dubrovskii [23] suggested a (2+1)-dimensional generalization of this equation,

4​Ut=U3​Us​s​s−3U​(U2​∂s−1(1U)y)y,4U_{t}=U^{3}U_{sss}-\frac{3}{U}\left(U^{2}\partial_{s}^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{U}\right)_{y}\right)_{y}, (1.9)

where ∂s−1\partial^{-1}_{s} is the formal anti-derivative with respect to ss. If UU does not depend on yy, the second term in the right-hand side vanishes and this equation converts into (1.8). One may say that the original HD equation (1.8) is related to its (2+1)-dimensional generalization (1.9) in the same way as the KdV equation is related to the KP equation. Like in the KP and mKP cases, the HD equation is the first member of an infinite hierarchy.

It is known that the three hierarchies have commutation representations of the Lax-Sato type. This formulation uses the well known notion of pseudo-differential operators. Consider the following pseudo-differential operators:

LKP=∂+u1∂−1+u2∂−2+…LmKP=∂+v0+v1∂−1+v2∂−2+…LHD=U∂+w0+w1∂−1+w2∂−2+…,\begin{array}[]{l}L^{\rm KP}=\partial+u_{1}\partial^{-1}+u_{2}\partial^{-2}+\ldots\\ \\ L^{\rm mKP}=\partial+v_{0}+v_{1}\partial^{-1}+v_{2}\partial^{-2}+\ldots\\ \\ L^{\rm HD}=U\partial+w_{0}+w_{1}\partial^{-1}+w_{2}\partial^{-2}+\ldots,\end{array} (1.10)

where ∂\partial is derivative with respect to some space variable (which is xx for KP and mKP and ss in the HD case). The functions ui,viu_{i},v_{i} in the first two lines are functions of xx while the functions UU and wiw_{i} in the third line are functions of ss. The first and the second ones are the Lax operators for the KP and mKP hierarchies respectively. The third one is the Lax operator for the HD hierarchy. In all the three cases, the commuting flows of the hierarchy are defined by the following Lax equations:

∂tnL=[(Ln)≥k,L],n≥2,\partial_{t_{n}}L=[(L^{n})_{\geq k},\,L],\quad n\geq 2, (1.11)

where k=0, 1, 2k=0,\,1,\,2 for the first, second and third cases respectively. (Hereafter we use the notation (∑nan∂n)≥k=∑n≥kan∂n(\sum\limits_{n}a_{n}\partial^{n})_{\geq k}=\sum\limits_{n\geq k}a_{n}\partial^{n}.) The Lax equations define a dynamics in the space of the pseudo-differential operators of the form (1.10) and the functions ui,vi,wiu_{i},v_{i},w_{i} and UU become functions not only of the space variable (xx or ss) but also of all the hierarchical times tnt_{n}.

The three hierarchies are known to be closely related. For example, in [12] Bäcklund-Darboux (BD) transformations were constructed between the three hierarchies, in addition to some auto-BD transformations. However, despite the fact that the first two hierarchies have been well studied from various points of view (for example, in terms of tau-functions and free fermions, for the review see, e.g., [24]), the same can not be said about the SchKP and HD hierarchies.

The main goal of this work is to fill some gaps in the theory of the SchKP and HD hierarchies and, in particular, to give their formulation in terms of tau-functions and bilinear equations for them. More precisely, we provide a new formulation of the SchKP hierarchy through a pair of KP tau-functions (τ^​(𝐭),τ¯​(𝐭))(\hat{\tau}({\bf t}),\bar{\tau}({\bf t})) (recall that where t1t_{1} is identified with the space variable xx) linked together by an additional bilinear equation. The main results can be summarized as the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1

Let τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) and τ¯​(𝐭)\bar{\tau}({\bf t}) be two KP tau-functions (i.e. solutions of equation (1.3)) such that they satisfy the bilinear equation

∮C∞eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​(τ^​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ¯​(𝐭′+[z−1])+τ¯​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ^​(𝐭′+[z−1]))​𝑑z=0\oint_{C_{\infty}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}},z)}\,\Bigl(\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\bar{\tau}({\bf t^{\prime}}+[z^{-1}])+\bar{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\hat{\tau}({\bf t^{\prime}}+[z^{-1}])\Bigr)dz=0 (1.12)

for all 𝐭{\bf t}, 𝐭′{\bf t}^{\prime}. Then, for all a1,a2,a3∈ℂa_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in\mbox{\Bbb C}, the function

S⁡(𝐭)=τ¯​(𝐭)τ^​(𝐭)S({\bf t})=\frac{\bar{\tau}({\bf t})}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})} (1.13)

solves the functional equation

(S[a1]−S[a1​a2])​(S[a2]−S[a2​a3])​(S[a3]−S[a1​a3])(S[a3]−S[a2​a3])​(S[a1]−S[a1​a3])​(S[a2]−S[a1​a2])=1,\frac{(S^{[a_{1}]}-S^{[a_{1}a_{2}]})(S^{[a_{2}]}-S^{[a_{2}a_{3}]})(S^{[a_{3}]}-S^{[a_{1}a_{3}]})}{(S^{[a_{3}]}-S^{[a_{2}a_{3}]})(S^{[a_{1}]}-S^{[a_{1}a_{3}]})(S^{[a_{2}]}-S^{[a_{1}a_{2}]})}=1, (1.14)

where S[ai]≡S⁡(𝐭−[ai−1])S^{[a_{i}]}\equiv S({\bf t}-[a_{i}^{-1}]), S[ai​aj]≡S⁡(𝐭−[ai−1]−[aj−1])S^{[a_{i}a_{j}]}\equiv S({\bf t}-[a_{i}^{-1}]-[a_{j}^{-1}]). In particular, it satisfies the SchKP equation (1.6) which is obtained from (1.14) in the limit a1,a2,a3→∞a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\to\infty.

Conversely, let S⁡(𝐭)S({\bf t}) be any solution to (1.14), then there exist two KP tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau}, τ¯\bar{\tau} such that the bilinear equation (1.12) holds and the function SS is given by (1.13).

Equation (1.14) is the generating functional equation of the SchKP hierarchy. Partial differential equations of the hierarchy are obtained by expanding its left-hand side in the Taylor series in inverse powers of a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3} and equating the coefficients to zero. In the leading non-vanishing order one obtains equation (1.6). At the same time, equation (1.6) can be interpreted as an integrable discretization of the SchKP equation. Namely, by setting S⁡(n1,n2,n3)=S⁡(𝐭−n1​[a1−1]−n2​[a2−1]−n3​[a3−1])S(n_{1},n_{2},n_{3})=S({\bf t}-n_{1}[a_{1}^{-1}]-n_{2}[a_{2}^{-1}]-n_{3}[a_{3}^{-1}]) for any fixed 𝐭{\bf t}, (1.6) converts into a discrete equation for S⁡(n1,n2,n3)S(n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}).

We also clarify the interrelation between the SchKP and HD hierarchies. The latter is nothing else than a reformulation of the former in terms of pseudo-differential operators (i.e., an equivalent formulation of the Lax-Sato type). This reformulation requires a nontrivial change of variables: the new space variable is s=S⁡(x)s=S(x), where is SS given by (1.13), so ∂x=Sx∂s\partial_{x}=S_{x}\partial_{s}, and U⁡(s)U(s) from (1.9) and (1.10) is defined as U=SxU=S_{x}. Besides, some previously known results about BD transformations are reformulated in terms of tau-functions. This allows them to be given a particularly simple and clear form.

Having mentioned BD transformations11 1 Sometimes they are called gauge transformations. of the integrable hierarchies, we should say that there is a huge literature devoted to this issue. (See, for example, [25]-[33] and references therein.) In turn, we could not but touch upon the issues related to this. In fact the language of BD transformations is especially convenient in analysis of the three hierarchies (1.1) and interrelations between them. The key notion in the theory of BD transformations is a wave function22 2 Some authors prefer to call them “eigenfunctions” but such terminology seems to be rather misleading because in general wave functions are not eigenfunctions of Lax operators. The name “wave function” that we use in this paper is motivated by the fact that the linear differential equation of the form (2.33) below for the t2t_{2}-flow formally coincides with the non-stationary Schredinger equation in imaginary time. for a given Lax operator (the one for KP, mKP or HD). For example, in the case of KP wave functions ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) are defined as common solutions to the equations

∂tnϕ⁡(𝐭)=Bn​ϕ​(𝐭),n≥2,\partial_{t_{n}}\phi({\bf t})=B_{n}\phi({\bf t}),\quad n\geq 2,

where BnB_{n} are differential operators Bn=(Ln)≥0B_{n}=(L^{n})_{\geq 0}. Given a solution to the KP hierarchy with a tau-function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}), the function τ^​(𝐭)=ϕ​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\phi({\bf t})\tau({\bf t}) is then another solution. This defines an (auto)BD transformation of the KP hierarchy and, simultaneously, a solution to the mKP herarchy, which is just given by the pair (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) of KP tau-functions. Moreover, any solution to the mKP hierarchy is defined in this way by a pair (τ,ϕ)(\tau,\phi), where τ\tau is a KP tau-function and ϕ\phi is a wave function associated with it (more precisely, with the Lax operator corresponding to this tau-function). This story can be further continued by considering wave functions for the mKP Lax operator LmKP=ℒL^{\rm mKP}={\cal L} corresponding to the solution (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}). Namely, let SS be such wave function, then τ¯=S​τ^\bar{\tau}=S\hat{\tau} is again a KP tau-function, and the pair (τ^,τ¯)(\hat{\tau},\bar{\tau}) solves the bilinear equation (1.12). Then S=τ¯/τ^S=\bar{\tau}/\hat{\tau} solves the SchKP equation (1.6). Moreover, any solution to the SchKP hierarchy is defined in this way by a pair (τ^,S)(\hat{\tau},S), where τ^\hat{\tau} is a KP tau-function and SS is a wave function for the mKP Lax operator associated with the solution (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}). Equivalently, to construct a solution to the SchKP hierarchy, one may start from two solutions to the mKP hierarchy: (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) (defined by fixing a wave function ϕ\phi) and (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) (defined by fixing another wave function ϕ′\phi^{\prime}) For clarity, all said above can be represented as the following diagram:

τ¯⟶ϕ¯τ¯^↑ϕ′↑ϕ^τ⟶ϕτ^\begin{array}[]{ccc}\bar{\tau}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bar{\phi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\bar{\tau}}\\ \uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle\phi^{\prime}}$\hss}&&\uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle\hat{\phi}}$\hss}\\ \tau&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\tau}\end{array} (1.15)

Note that the vertices correspond to solutions of KP, edges correspond to solutions to mKP, and the whole square (more precisely, the diagonal from τ¯\bar{\tau} to τ^\hat{\tau}) can be associated to a solution to SchKP (more precisely, two solutions: S=τ¯/τ^S=\bar{\tau}/\hat{\tau} and S−1=τ^/τ¯S^{-1}=\hat{\tau}/\bar{\tau}).

Lastly, we establish a close connection with multi-component KP hierarchy [39, 40, 41, 42].

Theorem 1.2

Let τ⁡(𝐬,𝐭)\tau({\bf s},{\bf t}), where 𝐬={s1,s2,s3}{\bf s}=\{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}\}, si∈ℤs_{i}\in\mbox{\Bbb Z} with the condition s1+s2+s3=0s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{3}=0, be the tau-function of the multi-component KP hierarchy restricted to the three-component sector, with all other discrete and continuous variables frozen. Then the pair of functions (τ⁡(0,0,0),τ⁡(0,1,−1))(\tau(0,0,0),\tau(0,1,-1)) solves equation (1.12) and thus provides a solution to the SchKP and HD hierarchies.

The outline of the paper is as follows. Section 2 is devoted to the well known KP hierarchy. We consider it both within the framework of bilinear formalism and the Lax-Sato approach, and provide a proof of their equivalence. All this is a basic preliminary stuff for what follows. A similar treatment of the mKP hierarchy is the subject of Section 3. The main idea here (which is not new), and also a useful technical tool, is realization of the mKP hierarchy as a chain of Bäcklund-Darboux transformations of solutions to the KP one. Section 4 is devoted to the SchKP and HD hierarchies. First, the SchKP hierarchy is obtained from considering Bäcklund-Darboux transformations of the mKP hierarchy (Section 4.1). Second, the bilinear approach to SchKP via a pair of KP tau-functions is developed. Third, it is shown that the reformulation in the framework of the Lax-Sato approach provides the HD hierarchy. In Section 5 the embedding of the SchKP hierarchy into the multi-component hierarchy is discussed. Section 6 contains some concluding remarks.

2 The KP hierarchy

The set of independent variables is 𝐭={t1,t2,t3,…}{\bf t}=\{t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},\ldots\}. The variable t1t_{1} can be identified with the space variable xx, so hereafter we put t1=xt_{1}=x. All other variables are interpreted as times associated with an infinite number of commuting flows.

In the bilinear formalism, the universal dependent variable is tau-function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}). The generating bilinear equation for the KP tau-function is of the form

∮C∞eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(𝐭′+[z−1])​𝑑z=0,\oint_{C_{\infty}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}])\,dz=0, (2.1)

where we the standard notation (1.4) is used. The contour C∞C_{\infty} is a big circle of radius R→∞R\to\infty around ∞\infty. Equation (2.1) is valid for all 𝐭{\bf t} and 𝐭′{\bf t}^{\prime}. The simplest possible solution (the trivial one) is τ⁡(𝐭)=1\tau({\bf t})=1. Note also that if τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) is a solution of (2.1), then eℓ⁡(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭)e^{\ell({\bf t})}\tau({\bf t}), where ℓ⁡(𝐭)\ell({\bf t}) is an arbitrary linear function of the times, is a solution, too. Two tau-functions that differ by such a factor are said to be equivalent.

Let us mention one of the most important corollaries of equation (2.1). Setting

𝐭−𝐭′=[a1−1]+[a2−1]+[a3−1],{\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}}=[a_{1}^{-1}]+[a_{2}^{-1}]+[a_{3}^{-1}],

where a1,a2,a3∈ℂa_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in\mbox{\Bbb C} are three different points, we have

eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)=a1​a2​a3(a1−z)​(a2−z)​(a3−z),e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}=\frac{a_{1}\,a_{2}\,a_{3}}{(a_{1}-z)(a_{2}-z)(a_{3}-z)},

and the integral in (2.1) can be calculated by an elementary residue calculus. The result is:

(a1−a2)​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1]−[a2−1])​τ​(𝐭−[a3−1])+(a2−a3)​τ​(𝐭−[a2−1]−[a3−1])​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1])+(a3−a1)​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1]−[a3−1])​τ​(𝐭−[a2−1])=0.\begin{array}[]{l}(a_{1}-a_{2})\tau({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]-[a_{2}^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}-[a_{3}^{-1}])\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaa}+\,(a_{2}-a_{3})\tau({\bf t}-[a_{2}^{-1}]-[a_{3}^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}])\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}+\,(a_{3}-a_{1})\tau({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]-[a_{3}^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}-[a_{2}^{-1}])=0.\end{array} (2.2)

This is the famous equation first obtained by Miwa [34]. As is proved in [35], it is in fact equivalent to the entire KP hierarchy defined by the integral equation (2.1) (see also [36] for the direct proof).

To write down such equations in a compact form, it is convenient to introduce some short-hand notation. Set

τ(𝐭−[aj−1])=τj,τ(𝐭−[aj−1]−[ak−1])=τj​k,etc,τ(𝐭+[aj−1])=τj,τ(𝐭+[aj−1]+[ak−1])=τj​k,etc.\begin{array}[]{l}\tau({\bf t}-[a_{j}^{-1}])=\tau^{j},\qquad\tau({\bf t}-[a_{j}^{-1}]-[a_{k}^{-1}])=\tau^{jk},\quad\mbox{etc},\\ \\ \tau({\bf t}+[a_{j}^{-1}])=\tau_{j},\qquad\tau({\bf t}+[a_{j}^{-1}]+[a_{k}^{-1}])=\tau_{jk},\quad\mbox{etc}.\end{array} (2.3)

Similar notation will be used for other functions of 𝐭{\bf t} introduced below (Baker-Akhiezer functions, wave functions, etc). This notation allows us to rewrite equation (2.2) in the following compact form:

a12​τ12​τ3+a23​τ23​τ1+a31​τ13​τ2=0,a_{12}\tau^{12}\tau^{3}+a_{23}\tau^{23}\tau^{1}+a_{31}\tau^{13}\tau^{2}=0, (2.4)

or, after an overall shift of 𝐭{\bf t},

a12​τ12​τ3+a23​τ23​τ1+a31​τ13​τ2=0a_{12}\tau_{12}\tau_{3}+a_{23}\tau_{23}\tau_{1}+a_{31}\tau_{13}\tau_{2}=0 (2.5)

(here and below ai​j≡ai−aja_{ij}\equiv a_{i}-a_{j}).

More generally, fix an integer m≥2m\geq 2, m+1m+1 distinct points ai∈ℂa_{i}\in\mbox{\Bbb C}, m−1m-1 distinct points bi∈ℂb_{i}\in\mbox{\Bbb C} and make the substitution

𝐭−𝐭′=∑i=1m+1[ai−1]−∑i=1m−1[bi−1].{\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}[a_{i}^{-1}]-\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}[b_{i}^{-1}]. (2.6)

Using residue calculus, we convert (2.1) into the following equation:

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​Δm​(a1,…,a^k,…,am+1)​∏i=1m−1(bi−ak)×τ⁡(𝐭−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])​τ​(𝐭−[ak−1]−∑j=1m−1[bj−1])=0\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\Delta_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{k},\ldots,a_{m+1})\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(b_{i}-a_{k})}\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\displaystyle{\times\,\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[a^{-1}_{k}]-\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}[b_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)=0}\end{array} (2.7)

(equation (2.2) is its particular case for m=2m=2, b1=∞b_{1}=\infty). Here

Δm​(a1,…,am)=det1≤i,j≤m(aim−j)=∏i<jm(ai−aj)\Delta_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})=\det_{1\leq i,j\leq m}(a_{i}^{m-j})=\prod_{i<j}^{m}(a_{i}-a_{j}) (2.8)

is the Vandermonde determinant, and a^k\hat{a}_{k} means that aka_{k} is omitted. Equations (2.7) can be written in the form which resembles Plücker relations. To this end, introduce the notation

τ⁡[a1,…,am]=Δm​(a1,…,am)​τ​(𝐭−∑j=1m[aj−1]).\tau\bigl[a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\bigr]=\Delta_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr). (2.9)

Clearly, τ⁡[a1,…,am]\tau\bigl[a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\bigr] is antisymmetric with respect to any permutation ai↔aka_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{k}. In this notation, equation (2.7) acquires the form

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​τ​[a1,…,a^k,…,am+1]​τ​[ak,b1,…,bm−1]=0.\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\tau\bigl[a_{1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{k},\ldots,a_{m+1}\bigr]\,\tau\bigl[a_{k},b_{1},\ldots,b_{m-1}\bigr]=0. (2.10)

Other important objects are Baker-Akhiezer33 3 This name is usually used in the context of algebraic-geometrical solutions to the KP hierarchy related to Riemann surfaces of finite genus. Here we extend this name to a broader class of solutions. (BA) function ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) and its adjoint (dual) ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\psi^{*}({\bf t},z). For any fixed values of the times, they are functions of a complex variable zz which is called spectral parameter. For the sake of brevity, we will sometimes refer to both ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) and ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\psi^{*}({\bf t},z) as BA functions, or simply ψ\psi-functions. In general, these functions, as functions of zz, are assumed to be holomorphic in a sufficiently small neighborhood 𝖴∞{\sf U}_{\infty} of ∞\infty (i.e., for |z|>R|z|>R with some sufficiently large RR) except maybe the very point z=∞z=\infty, where an essential singularity is allowed. In this neighborhood they can be expressed through the tau-function as follows:

ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])τ⁡(𝐭),ψ∗​(𝐭,z)=e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ⁡(𝐭+[z−1])τ⁡(𝐭).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\psi({\bf t},z)=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})},}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\frac{\tau({\bf t}+[z^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}.}\end{array} (2.11)

These remarkable formulas were obtained in [4, 5].

The expansions of the BA functions as z→∞z\to\infty are

ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​(1+ξ1​(𝐭)​z−1+ξ2​(𝐭)​z−2+…),ψ∗​(𝐭,z)=e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​(1+ξ1∗​(𝐭)​z−1+ξ2∗​(𝐭)​z−2+…).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\psi({\bf t},z)=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\Bigl(1+\xi_{1}({\bf t})z^{-1}+\xi_{2}({\bf t})z^{-2}+\ldots\,\Bigr),}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\Bigl(1+\xi^{*}_{1}({\bf t})z^{-1}+\xi^{*}_{2}({\bf t})z^{-2}+\ldots\,\Bigr).}\end{array} (2.12)

The coefficients ξk​(𝐭)\xi_{k}({\bf t}), ξk∗​(𝐭)\xi^{*}_{k}({\bf t}) can be expressed through logarithmic derivatives of the tau-function with respect to the tkt_{k}’s but we do not need these formulas here. Their dependence on the times is determined by a chosen solution of (2.1). It is explicitly specified in terms of partial differential equations given below. In terms of the BA functions, the bilinear equation (2.1) acquires the form

∮C∞ψ⁡(𝐭,z)​ψ∗​(𝐭′,z)​𝑑z=0.\oint_{C_{\infty}}\psi({\bf t},z)\psi^{*}({\bf t^{\prime}},z)\,dz=0. (2.13)

It holds for all 𝐭{\bf t}, 𝐭′{\bf t^{\prime}}.

Remark 2.1

The latter equation for the ψ\psi-functions can serve as a starting point of the theory. In particular, it implies existence of the tau-function, i.e., a function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) such that the ψ\psi-functions are expressed through it by means of formulas (2.11). The proof is given in [4].

It is worth noting that for some important classes of solutions the BA functions can be analytically continued outside 𝖴∞{\sf U}_{\infty} as analytic functions on ℂ∖𝖲\mbox{\Bbb C}\setminus{\sf S}, where 𝖲⊂ℂ{\sf S}\subset\mbox{\Bbb C} is a set of points of nonzero co-dimension (which is 22 for a number of isolated points or 11 for lines). (The well known examples are soliton and rational solutions.) To avoid unnecessary analytical complications in this work, we will have in mind the classes of solutions for which such analytic continuation is possible.

Remark 2.2

For completeness, let us say some words about the general case, when the BA functions can not be analytically continued from 𝖴∞{\sf U}_{\infty} to bigger domains of the complex plane. In this case ∂z¯ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\partial_{\bar{z}}\psi({\bf t},z) and ∂z¯ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\partial_{\bar{z}}\psi^{*}({\bf t},z) may be nonzero in some compact 2D domain 𝖣⊂ℂ{\sf D}\subset\mbox{\Bbb C}, and the BA functions (which are functions of both zz and z¯\bar{z} for 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁z∈𝖣)z\in{\sf D}) are characterized by certain integral or integro-diffrential equations which were suggested in [37] and are known in the literature as non-local ∂¯\bar{\partial}-problem. They are:

∂z¯ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=∫ℂK⁡(z,ζ)​ψ​(𝐭,ζ)​d2​ζ,∂z¯ψ∗(𝐭,z)=−∫ℂψ∗(𝐭,ζ)K(ζ,z)d2ζ.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\partial_{\bar{z}}\psi({\bf t},z)=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}K(z,\zeta)\psi({\bf t},\zeta)\,d^{2}\zeta,}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\partial_{\bar{z}}\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=-\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\psi^{*}({\bf t},\zeta)K(\zeta,z)\,d^{2}\zeta.}\end{array} (2.14)

The kernel K⁡(z,ζ)K(z,\zeta) is assumed to have a compact support with respect to the both arguments, i.e., K⁡(z,ζ)=0K(z,\zeta)=0 if zz or ζ\zeta belongs to 𝖴∞{\sf U}_{\infty}. This condition allows one to require the holomorphic in zz asymptotics as z→∞z\to\infty of the form (2.12). Under certain conditions imposed on the kernel these integro-differential equations are known to have nontrivial solutions, and the linear space of solutions is in general one-dimensional.

It is instructive to think of the BA function as the result of the action of a “dressing operator” WW to the simplest possible BA function eξ⁡(𝐭,z)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)} corresponding to the trivial solution. The operator WW is a pseudo-differential operator of order 0 of the form

W=1+ξ1∂x−1+ξ2∂x−2+…,W=1+\xi_{1}\partial_{x}^{-1}+\xi_{2}\partial_{x}^{-2}+\ldots, (2.15)

where ∂x=∂/∂x\partial_{x}=\partial/\partial x (recall that we identify x=t1x=t_{1}) and the coefficient functions ξk=ξk​(𝐭)\xi_{k}=\xi_{k}({\bf t}) are the same as in the first formula in (2.12). Clearly, we can write

ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=W​eξ⁡(𝐭,z),\psi({\bf t},z)=We^{\xi({\bf t},z)}, (2.16)

where it is implied that ∂x−1\partial_{x}^{-1} formally acts on ex​ze^{xz} as ∂x−1ex​z=z−1​ex​z\partial_{x}^{-1}e^{xz}=z^{-1}e^{xz}.

The dressing operator allows one to introduce the Lax operator LL of the KP hierarchy by “dressing” of the ∂x\partial_{x}:

L=W∂xW−1=∂x+u1∂x−1+u2∂x−2+….L=W\partial_{x}W^{-1}=\partial_{x}+u_{1}\partial_{x}^{-1}+u_{2}\partial_{x}^{-2}+\ldots\,. (2.17)

It is a pseudo-differential operator of order 1. The coefficient functions uiu_{i} can be expressed through logarithmic derivatives of the tau-function. Along with the Lax operator, we introduce the purely differential operators

Bk=(Lk)≥0,k≥1,B_{k}=(L^{k})_{\geq 0},\qquad k\geq 1, (2.18)

where for any subset 𝕊⊂ℤ\mbox{\Bbb S}\subset\mbox{\Bbb Z} the operation (…)𝕊(\ldots)_{\raise-1.0pt\hbox{$\mbox{\Bbbb S}$}} applied to any pseudo-differential operator P=∑j∈ℤpj∂xj\displaystyle{P=\sum_{j\in\raise-1.0pt\hbox{$\mbox{\Bbbb Z}$}}p_{j}\partial_{x}^{j}} is defined as

(P)𝕊=(∑jpj∂xj)𝕊=∑j∈𝕊pj∂xj.(P)_{\raise-1.0pt\hbox{$\mbox{\Bbbb S}$}}=\Bigl(\sum_{j}p_{j}\partial_{x}^{j}\Bigr)_{\raise-1.0pt\hbox{$\mbox{\Bbbb S}$}}=\sum_{j\in\raise-1.0pt\hbox{$\mbox{\Bbbb S}$}}p_{j}\partial_{x}^{j}.

For example, B1=∂xB_{1}=\partial_{x}, B2=∂x2+2u1B_{2}=\partial_{x}^{2}+2u_{1}.

Remarkably, the bilinear relation (2.13) for the ψ\psi-functions alone implicitly defines possible dynamics in the space of the coefficients uiu_{i} of the Lax operator making them certain functions of the times: ui=ui​(𝐭)u_{i}=u_{i}({\bf t}). This dynamics can be described by partial differential equations.

Theorem 2.1

([4]) Let ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z), ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\psi^{*}({\bf t},z) be functions of the form (2.12). If the bilinear relation (2.13) is satisfied, then there exists a dressing operator WW of the form (2.15) such that ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=W​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z)=We^{\xi({\bf t},z)} satisfying the evolution equations

∂tkW=−(Lk)<0​W​for any k≥1.\partial_{t_{k}}W=-(L^{k})_{<0}W\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}. (2.19)

Proof. The proof given below is borrowed from [4]. The following technical lemma is useful44 4 It is a simplified version of Lemma 1.1 from [4].:

Lemma 2.1

Let PP and QQ be monic pseudo-differential operators of the form

P=1+∑j≥1pj(x)∂x−j,Q=1+∑j≥1qj(x)(−∂x)−j.P=1+\sum_{j\geq 1}p_{j}(x)\partial_{x}^{-j},\quad Q=1+\sum_{j\geq 1}q_{j}(x)(-\partial_{x})^{-j}.

Then imposing the condition

∮C∞(Px​ex​z)​(Qx′​e−x′​z)​𝑑z=0\oint_{C_{\infty}}(P_{x}e^{xz})\,(Q_{x^{\prime}}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=0 (2.20)

for all x,x′x,x^{\prime} implies that

(P​Q†)<0=0.\Bigl(P\,Q^{{\dagger}}\Bigr)_{<0}=0. (2.21)

(The notation PxP_{x}, Qx′Q_{x^{\prime}} in (2.20) means that the operators act on functions of x,x′x,x^{\prime}, respectively.)

In (2.21), Q†Q^{{\dagger}} is the conjugated operator. The conjugation (…)†(\ldots)^{{\dagger}} of differential and pseudo-differential operators is defined as (f(x)∘∂x)†=−∂x∘f(x)(f(x)\circ\partial_{x})^{{\dagger}}=-\partial_{x}\circ f(x), or, more generally, if P=∑kpk∘∂xk\displaystyle{P=\sum_{k}p_{k}\circ\partial_{x}^{k}}, then Pk†=∑k(−∂x)k∘pk.\displaystyle{P^{{\dagger}}_{k}=\sum_{k}(-\partial_{x})^{k}\circ p_{k}.} For the proof of the lemma see [4] (Lemma 1.1).

Set

ψ⁡(𝐭,z)=W​eξ⁡(𝐭,z),ψ∗​(𝐭,z)=V​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z)=We^{\xi({\bf t},z)},\quad\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=Ve^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}

where both WW and VV are of the form (2.15). Plugging this into (2.13) with tk=tk′t_{k}=t^{\prime}_{k} for k≥2k\geq 2, we have:

∮C∞(Wx​ex​z)​(Vx′​e−x′​z)​𝑑z=0.\oint_{C_{\infty}}(W_{x}e^{xz})\,(V_{x^{\prime}}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=0.

Now we can apply Lemma 2.1 with P=WP=W, Q=VQ=V and conclude that (W​V†)<0=0(W\,V^{{\dagger}})_{<0}=0. Since the both operators are monic and contain non-positive powers of ∂x\partial_{x} only, this means that W​V†=1W\,V^{{\dagger}}=1, i.e.,

V=(W†)−1.V=(W^{{\dagger}})^{-1}. (2.22)

Next, define the operators LL and BkB_{k} as in (2.17) and (2.18). Then (2.13) implies:

∮C∞(∂tn−Bn)ψ(𝐭,z)ψ∗(𝐭′,z)dz=0.\oint_{C_{\infty}}(\partial_{t_{n}}-B_{n})\psi({\bf t},z)\psi^{*}({\bf t^{\prime}},z)\,dz=0. (2.23)

We have, using (2.16) and (2.17):

(∂tn−Bn)ψ(𝐭,z)=(∂tnW+W∂xn−BnW)eξ⁡(𝐭,z)(\partial_{t_{n}}-B_{n})\psi({\bf t},z)=(\partial_{t_{n}}W+W\partial_{x}^{n}-B_{n}W)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}
=(∂tnW+Ln​W−Bn​W)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(∂tnW+(Ln)<0​W)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z).=(\partial_{t_{n}}W+L^{n}W-B_{n}W)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=(\partial_{t_{n}}W+(L^{n})_{<0}W)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}.

Again, putting tk=tk′t_{k}=t_{k}^{\prime} for k≥2k\geq 2, we rewrite (2.23) as

∮C∞(R​ex​z)​((W†)−1​e−x′​z)​𝑑z=0,\oint_{C_{\infty}}(Re^{xz})\,((W^{{\dagger}})^{-1}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=0,

where RR is the operator R=∂tnW+(Ln)<0​WR=\partial_{t_{n}}W+(L^{n})_{<0}W. By Lemma 2.1, we conclude that (R​W−1)<0=0(R\,W^{-1})_{<0}=0. Clearly, RR contains strictly negative powers of ∂x\partial_{x} only and the same is true for the operator R​W−1R\,W^{-1}, i.e., (R​W−1)<0=R​W−1=0(R\,W^{-1})_{<0}=R\,W^{-1}=0. Since WW is a monic operator, it follows from this that R=0R=0, which proves (2.19).  

Corollary 2.1

The function ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) is an eigenfunction of the Lax operator LL (2.17) with eigenvalue zz,

L​ψ​(𝐭,z)=z​ψ​(𝐭,z),L\psi({\bf t},z)=z\psi({\bf t},z), (2.24)

and for any z∈ℂz\in\mbox{\Bbb C} it satisfies the differential equations

∂tkψ⁡(𝐭,z)=Bk​ψ​(𝐭,z)​for any k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}\psi({\bf t},z)=B_{k}\psi({\bf t},z)\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (2.25)

where the kk-th order differential operators BkB_{k} of the form Bk=∂xk+∑j=0k−2bk∂xj\displaystyle{B_{k}=\partial_{x}^{k}+\sum_{j=0}^{k-2}b_{k}\partial_{x}^{j}} are given by equation (2.18).

Proof. Again, we follow [4]. The eigenvalue equation (2.24) is a trivial consequence of (2.16), (2.17). Equation (2.25) easily follows from (2.19):

∂tkψ⁡(𝐭,z)=∂tkW​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)+W​zk​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=−(Lk)<0​W​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)+W​∂xkeξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(−(Lk)<0+Lk)​W​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(Lk)≥0​ψ​(𝐭,z).\begin{array}[]{lll}\partial_{t_{k}}\psi({\bf t},z)&=&\partial_{t_{k}}W\,e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}+Wz^{k}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\\ &&\\ &=&-(L^{k})_{<0}We^{\xi({\bf t},z)}+W\partial_{x}^{k}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\\ &&\\ &=&\Bigl(-(L^{k})_{<0}+L^{k}\Bigr)We^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=(L^{k})_{\geq 0}\psi({\bf t},z).\end{array}
 

In what follows, by the BA function we mean a function of the form (2.12) such that it satisfies equations (2.24) and (2.25). Theorem 2.1 implies that this definition is equivalent to the first formula in (2.11), where the tau-function satisfies (2.1).

There are similar statements for the adjoint BA function ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\psi^{*}({\bf t},z). From the proof of Theorem 2.1 we already know that

ψ∗​(𝐭,z)=(W†)−1​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z).\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=(W^{{\dagger}})^{-1}e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}. (2.26)

An easy calculation that uses equation (2.19) shows that the adjoint BA function satisfies linear equations which are conjugated to those for ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) (see (2.24), (2.25)).

Corollary 2.2

The function ψ∗​(𝐭,z)\psi^{*}({\bf t},z) is the adjoint BA function, i.e., it satisfies the equations

L†​ψ∗​(𝐭,z)=z​ψ∗​(𝐭,z),L^{{\dagger}}\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=z\psi^{*}({\bf t},z), (2.27)
−∂tkψ∗(𝐭,z)=Bk†ψ∗(𝐭,z)for any k≥1.-\partial_{t_{k}}\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)=B^{{\dagger}}_{k}\psi^{*}({\bf t},z)\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}. (2.28)
 
Remark 2.3

Taking into account equations (2.11), we can represent the dressing operator WW as

W=∙∙​τ(𝐭−[∂x−1])τ⁡(𝐭)​∙∙,(W†)−1=∙∙​τ(𝐭+[∂x−1])τ⁡(𝐭)​∙∙,W={\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}}\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}{\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}},\qquad(W^{{\dagger}})^{-1}={\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}}\frac{\tau({\bf t}+[\partial_{x}^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}{\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}}, (2.29)

where the normal ordering means that operator ∂x\partial_{x} in each term of the expansion in negative powers of ∂x−1\partial_{x}^{-1} is moved to the right. Note that the second equality is by no means an algebraic consequence of the first one. It holds only on condition that τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) is a KP tau-function, i.e., satisfies the bilinear equation (2.1).

The following well known proposition directly links the tau-function and the Lax operator.

Proposition 2.1

Let LL be the Lax operator of the KP hierarchy. The coefficient at ∂x−1\partial_{x}^{-1} of the pseudo-differential operator LnL^{n} (sometimes called the operator residue of the pseudo-differential operator LnL^{n}) is expressed through the tau-function as follows:

(Ln)−1=∂tn∂xlog⁡τ,n≥1.(L^{n})_{-1}=\partial_{t_{n}}\partial_{x}\log\tau,\quad n\geq 1. (2.30)

This relation can be proved by applying the differential operator ∂tn\partial_{t_{n}} to the bilinear relation (2.1) and putting 𝐭′=𝐭{\bf t^{\prime}}={\bf t} afterwords. Details of the proof can be found e.g. in [38].

As is well known, compatibility of equations (2.24), (2.25) (or (2.27), (2.28)) implies the Lax equations

∂tkL=[Bk,L],k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}L=[B_{k},L],\quad k\geq 1, (2.31)

and the Zakharov-Shabat equations

∂tnBm−∂tmBn+[Bm,Bn]=0,n,m≥1.\partial_{t_{n}}B_{m}-\partial_{t_{m}}B_{n}+[B_{m},B_{n}]=0,\quad n,m\geq 1. (2.32)

The latter are in fact compatibility conditions for the Lax equations (2.31). They determine dynamics in the space of dependent variables. Usually, these equations serve as a definition of the KP hierarchy.

An important role in the theory is played by wave functions.

Definition 2.1

Any solution ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) to the system of linear differential equations (2.25), i.e.,

∂tkϕ⁡(𝐭,z)=Bk​ϕ​(𝐭,z)​for any k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}\phi({\bf t},z)=B_{k}\phi({\bf t},z)\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (2.33)

is called a wave function (for the KP hierarchy). Any solution ϕ∗​(𝐭)\phi^{*}({\bf t}) to the conjugated system of equations (2.28), i.e.,

−∂tkϕ∗(𝐭,z)=Bk†ϕ∗(𝐭,z)for any k≥1,-\partial_{t_{k}}\phi^{*}({\bf t},z)=B^{{\dagger}}_{k}\phi^{*}({\bf t},z)\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (2.34)

is called an adjoint wave function.

For brevity, we will call both ϕ\phi and ϕ∗\phi^{*} wave functions, if this does not lead to a misunderstanding.

Note that the BA functions (adjoint BA functions) are particular and very special solutions to the linear system (2.33) (respectively, (2.34)). Namely, they are simultaneously eigenfunctions of the Lax operator. However, the whole set of wave functions is much broader. Indeed, since the linear equations (2.25) and (2.28) do not contain the spectral parameter zz explicitly, any linear combination of BA functions ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) for different values of zz is a wave function. So, wave functions ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}), ϕ∗​(𝐭)\phi^{*}({\bf t}) can be constructed by integrating the BA functions with respect to the spectral parameter zz with arbitrary functions (in general, distributions) ρ⁡(z)\rho(z), ρ∗​(z)\rho^{*}(z) of z,z¯z,\bar{z} (we call them density functions):

ϕ⁡(𝐭)=∫ℂψ⁡(𝐭,z)​ρ​(z)​d2​z,ϕ∗​(𝐭)=∫ℂψ∗​(𝐭,z)​ρ∗​(z)​d2​z,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\phi({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\psi({\bf t};z)\rho(z)d^{2}z,}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\phi^{*}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\psi^{*}({\bf t};z)\rho^{*}(z)d^{2}z,}\end{array} (2.35)

where d2​z≡d​x​d​yd^{2}z\equiv dxdy is the standard measure in the complex plane55 5 We assume that the density functions ρ⁡(z)\rho(z), ρ∗​(z)\rho^{*}(z) are such that the integrals converge; for example, we may require that they are bounded and have a compact support.. Below we will deal with equations (2.35) rewritten in terms of the tau-function:

ϕ⁡(𝐭)=1τ⁡(𝐭)​∫ℂd2​z​ρ​(z)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1]),ϕ∗​(𝐭)=1τ⁡(𝐭)​∫ℂd2​z​ρ∗​(z)​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ​(𝐭+[z−1]).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\phi({\bf t})=\frac{1}{\tau({\bf t})}\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}d^{2}z\,\rho(z)\,e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]\Bigr),}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\phi^{*}({\bf t})=\frac{1}{\tau({\bf t})}\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}d^{2}z\,\rho^{*}(z)\,e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\tau\Bigl({\bf t}+[z^{-1}]\Bigr).}\end{array} (2.36)

The following proposition proved in [30] states that formulas (2.35) provide in fact general solution to the linear equations (2.33), (2.34).

Proposition 2.2

[30] Any KP wave function, i.e., a common solution to the linear equations (2.33) (or (2.34) for adjoint wave functions) have integral representation of the form (2.35) with some density functions (more generally, distributions) ρ\rho, ρ∗\rho^{*}.

Moreover, in [30] some explicit formulas which allow one to restore density functions from known wave functions were given. We will not present them here since we do not need them in what follows.

There are the following main possibilities for the density function:

  • –

    The support of ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) is a compact domain 𝖣∈ℂ{\sf D}\in\mbox{\Bbb C}: ρ⁡(z)=μ⁡(z)​Θ𝖣​(z),\rho(z)=\mu(z)\Theta_{\sf D}(z), where μ⁡(z)\mu(z) is a bounded function of z,z¯z,\bar{z} and Θ𝖣​(z)\Theta_{\sf D}(z) is the characteristic function of the domain 𝖣{\sf D}: Θ𝖣​(z)=1\Theta_{\sf D}(z)=1 if z∈𝖣z\in{\sf D} and 00 otherwise. In this case we encounter the non-local ∂¯\bar{\partial}-problem, as explained in Remark 2.2. We do not consider this case in this paper and hope to address it elsewhere.

  • –

    The support of ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) is a contour Γ⊂ℂ\Gamma\subset\mbox{\Bbb C}, and ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) is a distribution represented in terms of the delta-function δΓ​(z)\delta_{\Gamma}(z) with the support on Γ\Gamma as follows66 6 The delta-function δΓ​(z)\delta_{\Gamma}(z) is defined by the rule ∫ℂf⁡(z)​δΓ​(z)​d2​z=∫Γf⁡(z)​|𝑑z|\displaystyle{\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}f(z)\delta_{\Gamma}(z)d^{2}z=\int_{\Gamma}f(z)|dz|} for any integrable function ff.: ρ⁡(z)=ν⁡(z)​δΓ​(z),\rho(z)=\nu(z)\delta_{\Gamma}(z), where ν⁡(z)\nu(z) is some integrable function.

  • –

    The support of ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) is a finite number of points pi∈ℂp_{i}\in\mbox{\Bbb C}, and ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) is a distribution represented as a linear combination of 2D delta-functions: ρ⁡(z)=∑ici​δ(2)​(z−pi).\displaystyle{\rho(z)=\sum_{i}c_{i}\delta^{(2)}(z-p_{i})}.

Various combinations of these types of density functions are also possible. The same is assumed for ρ∗​(z)\rho^{*}(z).

3 Modified KP hierarchy

3.1 Modified KP from Toda lattice

To introduce the modified KP (mKP) hierarchy, it is instructive to begin with the more general 2D Toda lattice (2DTL) hierarchy. The independent variables of the latter are two infinite sets of times

𝐭={t1,t2,t3,…},𝐭¯={t¯1,t¯2,t¯3,…}{\bf t}=\{t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},\ldots\},\quad\bar{\bf t}=\{\bar{t}_{1},\bar{t}_{2},\bar{t}_{3},\ldots\}

(the bar here does not mean complex conjugation!) and a discrete variable n∈ℤn\in\mbox{\Bbb Z}. The universal dependent variable is the 2D Toda tau-function τ⁡(n,𝐭,𝐭¯)\tau(n,{\bf t},\bar{\bf t}) which satisfies the bilinear equation

∮C∞d​z​zn−n′−1​eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(n,𝐭−[z−1],𝐭¯)​τ​(n′+1,𝐭′+[z−1],𝐭′¯)=∮C∞d​z​zn′−n−1​eξ⁡(𝐭¯−𝐭¯′,z)​τ​(n+1,𝐭,𝐭¯−[z−1])​τ​(n′,𝐭′,𝐭′¯+[z−1]).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\oint_{C_{\infty}}dz\,z^{n-n^{\prime}-1}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau(n,{\bf t}-[z^{-1}],\,\bar{\bf t})\tau(n^{\prime}+1,{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}],\,\bar{\bf t^{\prime}})}\\ \\ \hskip-11.38109pt=\,\displaystyle{\oint_{C_{\infty}}dz\,z^{n^{\prime}-n-1}e^{\xi(\bar{\bf t}-\bar{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau(n+1,{\bf t},\,\bar{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau(n^{\prime},{\bf t}^{\prime},\,\bar{\bf t^{\prime}}+[z^{-1}]).}\end{array} (3.1)

It is valid for all 𝐭,𝐭′{\bf t},\,{\bf t^{\prime}}, 𝐭¯,𝐭′¯\bar{\bf t},\,\bar{\bf t^{\prime}} and n,n′∈ℤn,\,n^{\prime}\in\mbox{\Bbb Z}.

For the choice 𝐭′¯=𝐭¯\bar{\bf t^{\prime}}=\bar{\bf t}, n′=n−1n^{\prime}=n-1 the right-hand side vanishes and equation (3.1) for τ⁡(n,𝐭,𝐭¯)\tau(n,{\bf t},\bar{\bf t}), regarded as a function of 𝐭{\bf t} with fixed 𝐭¯\bar{\bf t} and nn, reduces to the bilinear equation (2.1) for the KP hierarchy.

For the choice 𝐭′¯=𝐭¯\bar{\bf t^{\prime}}=\bar{\bf t}, n−n′=k+1n-n^{\prime}=k+1 with k≥1k\geq 1 the right-hand side vanishes again and the equation becomes

∮C∞dzzkeξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)τ(n+k,𝐭−[z−1])τ(n,𝐭′+[z−1])=0,k≥1,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\oint_{C_{\infty}}dz\,z^{k}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau(n+k,{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau(n,{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}])=0,\quad k\geq 1,}\end{array} (3.2)

where we omitted dependence on the bar-times which enter implicitly as parameters of solutions. The hierarchy defined by equation (3.2) is sometimes referred to as the kk-modified KP hierarchy (kk-mKP). In what follows, we will deal with the most important case k=1k=1. This is just the mKP hierarchy in the Kupershmidt and Kiso sense. At k=0k=0 the KP hierarchy is reproduced.

Note that for the choice 𝐭′¯=𝐭¯\bar{\bf t^{\prime}}=\bar{\bf t}, n−n′=0n-n^{\prime}=0 in (3.1) (corresponding to k=−1k=-1) the right-hand side of (3.1) does not vanish but can be easily found explicitly as given by the residue at ∞\infty:

12​π​i​∮C∞d​zz​eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(n,𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(n+1,𝐭′+[z−1])=τ⁡(n+1,𝐭)​τ​(n,𝐭′).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{C_{\infty}}\frac{dz}{z}\,e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau(n,{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau(n+1,{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}])=\tau(n+1,{\bf t})\,\tau(n,{\bf t^{\prime}}).}\end{array} (3.3)

This equation (or rather functional relation) as well as (3.2) for k=1k=1, connects two neighboring tau-functions on the nn-lattice and is in fact equivalent to it defining the same mKP hierarchy77 7 This can be proved using the method developed in [36]..

Since in what follows we will not be interested in dependence on nn, it is convenient to fix them and simplify the notation as follows:

τ⁡(n,𝐭)=τ⁡(𝐭),τ⁡(n+1,𝐭)=τ^​(𝐭).\tau(n,{\bf t})=\tau({\bf t}),\qquad\tau(n+1,{\bf t})=\hat{\tau}({\bf t}). (3.4)

From what was said above it is clear that both functions τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) and τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) are KP tau-functions and, as such, satisfy equation (2.1). The mKP hierarchy contains the extra equation (3.3) that connects them:

12​π​i​∮C∞d​zz​eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ^​(𝐭′+[z−1])=τ^​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭′).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{C_{\infty}}\frac{dz}{z}\,e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\hat{\tau}({\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}])=\hat{\tau}({\bf t})\,\tau({\bf t^{\prime}}).}\end{array} (3.5)

Let us mention some important corollaries of the general equation (3.5). Setting

𝐭−𝐭′=[a1−1]+[a2−1],{\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}}=[a_{1}^{-1}]+[a_{2}^{-1}],

we have

eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)=a1​a2(a1−z)​(a2−z),e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}=\frac{a_{1}\,a_{2}}{(a_{1}-z)(a_{2}-z)},

and the integral in (3.5) can be calculated by an elementary residue calculus. The result is:

a1​τ​(𝐭−[a2−1])​τ^​(𝐭−[a1−1])−a2​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1])​τ^​(𝐭−[a2−1])=(a1−a2)​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1]−[a2−1])​τ^​(𝐭).\begin{array}[]{l}a_{1}\tau({\bf t}-[a_{2}^{-1}])\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}])-a_{2}\tau({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}])\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[a_{2}^{-1}])\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}=(a_{1}-a_{2})\tau({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]-[a_{2}^{-1}])\hat{\tau}({\bf t}).\end{array} (3.6)

In the short-hand notation introduced in (2.3) this equation can be written in a much more compact form:

a1​τ2​τ^1−a2​τ1​τ^2=a12​τ12​τ^,a_{1}\tau^{2}\hat{\tau}^{1}-a_{2}\tau^{1}\hat{\tau}^{2}=a_{12}\tau^{12}\hat{\tau}, (3.7)

or, after an overall shift of 𝐭{\bf t},

a1​τ1​τ^2−a2​τ2​τ^1=a12​τ​τ^12.a_{1}\tau_{1}\hat{\tau}_{2}-a_{2}\tau_{2}\hat{\tau}_{1}=a_{12}\tau\hat{\tau}_{12}. (3.8)

As is proved in [36], equation (3.7) (or (3.8)) is in fact equivalent to the whole mKP hierarchy defined by the integral equation (3.5). There is a slightly more generally looking version of equation (3.7) including three rather than two points, which is sometimes useful. It is obtained from (3.5) in the same manner after the substitution 𝐭−𝐭′=[a1−1]+[a2−1]+[a3−1]{\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}}=[a_{1}^{-1}]+[a_{2}^{-1}]+[a_{3}^{-1}]:

(a1−1−a2−1)​τ12​τ^3+(a2−1−a3−1)​τ23​τ^1+(a3−1−a1−1)​τ13​τ^2=0.(a_{1}^{-1}-a_{2}^{-1})\tau^{12}\hat{\tau}^{3}+(a_{2}^{-1}-a_{3}^{-1})\tau^{23}\hat{\tau}^{1}+(a_{3}^{-1}-a_{1}^{-1})\tau^{13}\hat{\tau}^{2}=0. (3.9)

It is reduced to (3.7) in the limit a3→∞a_{3}\to\infty. (However, as it was already said, equations (3.7) and (3.9) are in fact equivalent to each other and to the entire hierarchy.)

Proposition 3.1

Let τ\tau, τ^\hat{\tau} be two functions satisfying equation (3.7) (or (3.8)). Then both of them are KP tau-functions, i.e., they satisfy equation (2.4).

Proof. Let us write equation (3.7) in the form

a12​τ12​τ^τ1​τ2=a1​τ^1τ1−a2​τ^2τ2a_{12}\frac{\tau^{12}\hat{\tau}}{\tau^{1}\tau^{2}}=a_{1}\frac{\hat{\tau}^{1}}{\tau^{1}}-a_{2}\frac{\hat{\tau}^{2}}{\tau^{2}}

and sum the three such equations written for the three cyclic permutations of (123)(123). Then the right-hand side vanishes, and we obtain (2.4). The argument for τ^\hat{\tau} is similar.  

Remark 3.1

Comparing equations (2.4) and (3.7), one can notice that the latter is formally obtained from the former in the “limit” a3→0a_{3}\to 0. More precisely, the following formal identification works:

τ⁡(n,𝐭−[z−1])|z=0→τ⁡(n+1,𝐭),orτ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])|z=0→τ^​(𝐭).\tau(n,{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\Bigr|_{z=0}\rightarrow\tau(n+1,{\bf t}),\quad\mbox{or}\quad\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\Bigr|_{z=0}\rightarrow\hat{\tau}({\bf t}). (3.10)

It is assumed here that the function τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]), as a function of zz, admits an analytic continuation to the point z=0z=0 from the neighborhood of ∞\infty, where it was originally defined. The rule (3.10) can be most easily understood in the language of free fermions (see, e.g., [24])).

3.2 From KP to modified KP and back

The transition τ​(𝐭)→τ^​(𝐭)\tau({\bf t})\rightarrow\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) is referred to as a Bäcklund-Darboux (BD) transformation of solutions to the KP hierarchy. So, the mKP hierarchy (3.3) describes chains of successive BD transformations. In what follows, the objects related to the solution with the tau-function τ^\hat{\tau} will be denoted by the same letters with hat (W^\hat{W}, L^\hat{L}, ψ^​(𝐭,z)\hat{\psi}({\bf t},z), ϕ^​(𝐭)\hat{\phi}({\bf t}), etc), the latter is a wave function for the solution with the tau-function τ^\hat{\tau}.

Theorem 3.1 below provides description of a general solution to the mKP hierarchy in the form (3.5). In plain words, all solutions to the mKP hierarchy can be constructed from a solution to the KP hierarchy and a wave function corresponding to it.

Theorem 3.1

a) Let τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) be a tau-function of the KP hierarchy (i.e., a solution to (2.1)), and ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) be a wave function corresponding to this solution. Then the function

τ^​(𝐭)=ϕ​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\phi({\bf t})\tau({\bf t}) (3.11)

is another KP tau-function (i.e., it solves (2.1), too) and the pair (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) satisfies equation (3.5).

b) Conversely, let a pair (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) of KP tau-functions be a solution to the mKP bilinear equation (3.5), then their ratio

ϕ⁡(𝐭)=τ^​(𝐭)τ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t})=\frac{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})}{\tau({\bf t})} (3.12)

is a KP wave function corresponding to the solution τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}).

Proof. The part a) is well known and is traced back to early works on BD transformations of integrable hierarchies (for a detailed proof see, e.g., the recent review [33] and references therein).

Here we give a sketch of proof of part b). We need to prove that the function ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) defined by (3.12) satisfies the linear equations (2.33) with the differential operators Bk=(Lk)≥0B_{k}=(L^{k})_{\geq 0}, where the Lax operator LL corresponds to the solution with the tau-function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}). To this end, we employ the method first suggested in [35] and then used in [42] for the multi-component KP hierarchy.

Introduce the differential operator

D(z)=∑k≥1z−kk∂tk,D(z)=\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{z^{-k}}{k}\,\partial_{t_{k}}, (3.13)

then for any function f⁡(𝐭)f({\bf t}) we can write f⁡(𝐭±[z−1])=e±D⁡(z)​f​(𝐭)f({\bf t}\pm[z^{-1}])=e^{\pm D(z)}f({\bf t}). We have to show that

D⁡(a)​ϕ​(𝐭)=∑k≥1a−kk​Bk​ϕ​(𝐭),D(a)\phi({\bf t})=\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{a^{-k}}{k}\,B_{k}\phi({\bf t}),

with ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) given by (3.12) and BkB_{k} being the differential operator in xx of kk-th order given by (2.18).

To this end, we note that the function ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) defined as the ration of KP tau-functions (3.12) satisfies the linear equation for the ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}):

a1​ϕ2−a2​ϕ1=a12​τ​τ12τ1​τ2​ϕ12.a_{1}\phi_{2}-a_{2}\phi_{1}=a_{12}\frac{\tau\tau_{12}}{\tau_{1}\tau_{2}}\,\phi_{12}. (3.14)

This immediately follows from equation (3.8) after the substitution τ^=τ​ϕ\hat{\tau}=\tau\phi. Letting a2→∞a_{2}\to\infty (and renaming a1=aa_{1}=a), we convert it into the following linear differential-difference equation:

(1−e−D⁡(a))ϕ(𝐭)=a−1(∂x−∂xlogτ⁡(𝐭−[a−1])τ⁡(𝐭))ϕ(𝐭),\Bigl(1-e^{-D(a)}\Bigr)\phi({\bf t})=a^{-1}\left(\partial_{x}-\partial_{x}\log\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[a^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}\right)\phi({\bf t}), (3.15)

or

a(1−e−D⁡(a))ϕ(𝐭)−(∂x−V(𝐭,a))ϕ(𝐭)=0,a\Bigl(1-e^{-D(a)}\Bigr)\phi({\bf t})-\Bigl(\partial_{x}-V({\bf t},a)\Bigr)\phi({\bf t})=0, (3.16)

where

V⁡(𝐭,a)=∂xlog⁡τ⁡(𝐭−[a−1])τ⁡(𝐭)=∑k≥1Vk​(𝐭)​a−k.V({\bf t},a)=\partial_{x}\log\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[a^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}=\sum_{k\geq 1}V_{k}({\bf t})a^{-k}. (3.17)

The functions Vk​(𝐭)V_{k}({\bf t}) are expressed through logarithmic derivatives of the tau-function τ\tau.

The next step is to find action of D⁡(a)D(a) on the BA function. This can be done in the following way. The starting point is the well known Hirota-Miwa three-term bilinear relation for the KP tau-function (2.5) (which is in fact equivalent to the whole hierarchy, see [36] for a direct proof). Putting a3=za_{3}=z and using formula (2.11) for the BA function, this relation can be represented in the form a linear equation for the BA function:

a1​ψ​(𝐭+[a2−1],z)−a2​ψ​(𝐭+[a1−1],z)=(a1−a2)​τ⁡(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭+[a1−1]+[a2−1])τ⁡(𝐭+[a1−1])​τ​(𝐭+[a2−1])​ψ​(𝐭+[a1−1]+[a2−1])a_{1}\psi({\bf t}+[a_{2}^{-1}],z)-a_{2}\psi({\bf t}+[a_{1}^{-1}],z)=(a_{1}-a_{2})\frac{\tau({\bf t})\tau({\bf t}+[a_{1}^{-1}]+[a_{2}^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t}+[a_{1}^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}+[a_{2}^{-1}])}\,\psi({\bf t}+[a_{1}^{-1}]+[a_{2}^{-1}]) (3.18)

(see [33] for details). Letting a2→∞a_{2}\to\infty (and renaming a1=aa_{1}=a), we convert it into the following linear differential-difference equation for the BA function:

a(1−e−D⁡(a))ψ(𝐭,z)−(∂x−V(𝐭,a))ψ(𝐭,z)=0,a\Bigl(1-e^{-D(a)}\Bigr)\psi({\bf t},z)-\Bigl(\partial_{x}-V({\bf t},a)\Bigr)\psi({\bf t},z)=0, (3.19)

which is the same as equation (3.16) for the ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}).

The operator e−D⁡(a)−1e^{-D(a)}-1 can be expanded as

e−D⁡(a)−1=∑k≥1pk(−[∂x−1])a−k,e^{-D(a)}-1=\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}(-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])a^{-k}, (3.20)

where pk​(𝐭)p_{k}({\bf t}) are elementary Schur polynomials defined by

exp⁡(∑k≥1tk​zk)=1+∑k≥1pk​(𝐭)​zk.\exp\Bigl(\sum_{k\geq 1}t_{k}z^{k}\Bigr)=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}({\bf t})z^{k}.

Their general structure is pk​(𝐭)=tk+Pk​(tk−1,…,t1),p_{k}({\bf t})=t_{k}+P_{k}(t_{k-1},\ldots,t_{1}), where PkP_{k} is a polynomial of the variables tlt_{l} with l<kl<k. For example,

p1(𝐭)=t1,p2(𝐭)=t2+12t12,p3(𝐭)=t3+t1t2+16t13,\begin{array}[]{l}p_{1}({\bf t})=t_{1},\quad p_{2}({\bf t})=t_{2}+\frac{1}{2}t_{1}^{2},\quad p_{3}({\bf t})=t_{3}+t_{1}t_{2}+\frac{1}{6}t_{1}^{3},\end{array}

so

p1(−[∂x−1])=−∂t1,p2(−[∂x−1])=12(−∂t2+∂t12),p3(−[∂x−1])=13(−∂t3+32∂t2∂t1−12∂t13).\begin{array}[]{l}p_{1}(-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])=-\partial_{t_{1}},\\ \\ p_{2}(-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])=\frac{1}{2}(-\partial_{t_{2}}+\partial_{t_{1}}^{2}),\\ \\ p_{3}(-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])=\frac{1}{3}(-\partial_{t_{3}}+\frac{3}{2}\partial_{t_{2}}\partial_{t_{1}}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{t_{1}}^{3}).\end{array}

Then from equation (3.16) it follows that the function ϕ\phi satisfies linear differential equations of the form

pk+1​(−∂~)​ϕ−Vk​ϕ=0,k≥1.p_{k+1}(-\tilde{\partial})\phi-V_{k}\phi=0,\qquad k\geq 1. (3.21)

To identify them with (2.33), we note that, as it follows from (3.19), the KP BA function ψ⁡(𝐭,z)\psi({\bf t},z) given by (2.11) satisfies the same equations

pk+1​(−∂~)​ψ−Vk​ψ=0,k≥1.p_{k+1}(-\tilde{\partial})\psi-V_{k}\psi=0,\qquad k\geq 1. (3.22)

The structure of these equations allows one to express the derivative ∂tkψ\partial_{t_{k}}\psi through derivatives ∂tlψ\partial_{t_{l}}\psi with l<kl<k:

∂tkψ=𝖡k(∂tk−1,…,∂t1)ψ,\partial_{t_{k}}\psi={\sf B}_{k}(\partial_{t_{k-1}},\ldots,\partial_{t_{1}})\psi, (3.23)

where 𝖡k{\sf B}_{k} in the right-hand side is some differential operator in the variables t1,…,tk−1t_{1},\ldots,t_{k-1}. Applying it successively for k=2,3,…k=2,3,\ldots, it is possible to represent the right-hand side of (3.23) as a differential operator containing ∂t1=∂x\partial_{t_{1}}=\partial_{x} only:

∂tkψ=Bk(∂x)ψ.\partial_{t_{k}}\psi=B_{k}(\partial_{x})\psi.

However, we already know from Corollary 2.1 that for the BA function the operators Bk(∂x)B_{k}(\partial_{x}) coincide with the operators ℬk{\cal B}_{k} defined in (2.18) (see (2.25)). Since the function ϕ\phi satisfies the same linear equations as the BA function ψ\psi, we conclude that from (3.16) it follows that ∂tkϕ=Bk​ϕ\partial_{t_{k}}\phi=B_{k}\phi, i.e., ϕ\phi defined in (3.12) is indeed a KP wave function.  

Equation (3.11) defines what is called forward BD transformation (of the KP hierarchy). A backward one is defined in a similar way with the help of any adjoint wave function ϕ∗​(𝐭)\phi^{*}({\bf t}):

τ^∗​(𝐭)=ϕ∗​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭),\hat{\tau}^{*}({\bf t})=\phi^{*}({\bf t})\tau({\bf t}), (3.24)

or, using (2.36),

τ^∗​(𝐭)=∫ℂρ∗​(z)​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ​(𝐭+[z−1])​𝑑z.\hat{\tau}^{*}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\rho^{*}(z)e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\tau({\bf t}+[z^{-1}])\,dz. (3.25)

More details can be found, e.g., in [33]. Here we just mention that the Lax operator LL for the forward BD transformation τ→τ^=ϕ​τ\tau\to\hat{\tau}=\phi\tau is transformed as follows:

L⟶ϕ​∂xϕ−1​L​ϕ​∂x−1ϕ−1L\longrightarrow\,\phi\partial_{x}\phi^{-1}L\phi\partial_{x}^{-1}\phi^{-1} (3.26)

(see [12] for details).

We conclude this section by presenting nonlinear equations satisfied by the functions ϕ\phi and ϕ∗\phi^{*}.

Theorem 3.2

The KP wave functions ϕ\phi and ϕ∗\phi^{*} satisfy the equations

a1​ϕ2−a2​ϕ1ϕ12+a2​ϕ3−a3​ϕ2ϕ23+a3​ϕ1−a1​ϕ3ϕ13=0,\frac{a_{1}\phi_{2}-a_{2}\phi_{1}}{\phi_{12}}+\frac{a_{2}\phi_{3}-a_{3}\phi_{2}}{\phi_{23}}+\frac{a_{3}\phi_{1}-a_{1}\phi_{3}}{\phi_{13}}=0, (3.27)
a2​ϕ12∗−a3​ϕ13∗ϕ1∗+a3​ϕ23∗−a1​ϕ12∗ϕ2∗+a1​ϕ13∗−a2​ϕ23∗ϕ3∗=0,\frac{a_{2}\phi^{*}_{12}-a_{3}\phi^{*}_{13}}{\phi^{*}_{1}}+\frac{a_{3}\phi^{*}_{23}-a_{1}\phi^{*}_{12}}{\phi^{*}_{2}}+\frac{a_{1}\phi^{*}_{13}-a_{2}\phi^{*}_{23}}{\phi^{*}_{3}}=0, (3.28)

which are the discrete mKP equations.

Proof. To prove (3.27), we rewrite equation (3.14) in the form

a1​ϕ2−a2​ϕ1ϕ12=a12​τ3​τ12​ττ1​τ2​τ3.\frac{a_{1}\phi_{2}-a_{2}\phi_{1}}{\phi_{12}}=a_{12}\,\frac{\tau_{3}\tau_{12}\tau}{\tau_{1}\tau_{2}\tau_{3}}.

Summing three such equations corresponding to cyclic permutations of (123)(123) and using (2.5), we obtain (3.27). Equation (3.28) can be proved in a similar way.  

Remark 3.2

Note that ϕ−1\phi^{-1} satisfies the same equation (3.28) as ϕ∗\phi^{*}. Therefore, if ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) is any wave function corresponding to the Lax operator LL of the KP hierarchy, then ϕ−1​(𝐭)\phi^{-1}({\bf t}) is an adjoint wave function for the Lax operator L^\hat{L} in the sense of Definition 2.1.

Let us present some other forms of equations (3.27), (3.28). According to the remark above, it is enough to write the equations for ϕ\phi. First of all, after overall shifts of the variables, equation (3.27) can be written as

a1​ϕ31−a2​ϕ32ϕ3+a2​ϕ12−a3​ϕ13ϕ1+a3​ϕ23−a1​ϕ12ϕ2=0.\frac{a_{1}\phi^{31}-a_{2}\phi^{32}}{\phi^{3}}+\frac{a_{2}\phi^{12}-a_{3}\phi^{13}}{\phi^{1}}+\frac{a_{3}\phi^{23}-a_{1}\phi^{12}}{\phi^{2}}=0. (3.29)

A direct calculation shows that this is the same as

|1a1​ϕ1ϕ23​ϕ11a2​ϕ2ϕ13​ϕ21a3​ϕ3ϕ12​ϕ3|=0.\left|\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&a_{1}\phi^{1}&\phi^{23}\phi^{1}\\ &&\\ 1&a_{2}\phi^{2}&\phi^{13}\phi^{2}\\ &&\\ 1&a_{3}\phi^{3}&\phi^{12}\phi^{3}\end{array}\right|=0. (3.30)

To write down another useful form of this equation, we denote

R⁡(α,β)=aα​ϕα−aβ​ϕβϕ,α,β=1,2,3,R(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{a_{\alpha}\phi^{\alpha}-a_{\beta}\phi^{\beta}}{\phi},\quad\alpha,\beta=1,2,3, (3.31)

then (3.29) can be written as R3​(1,2)+R1​(2,3)+R2​(3,1)=0.R^{3}(1,2)+R^{1}(2,3)+R^{2}(3,1)=0. Moreover, a direct calculation shows that this is equivalent to

Rγ​(α,β)R⁡(α,β)=Rα​(β,γ)R⁡(β,γ),(αβγ)=(123),(231),(312).\frac{R^{\gamma}(\alpha,\beta)}{R(\alpha,\beta)}=\frac{R^{\alpha}(\beta,\gamma)}{R(\beta,\gamma)},\qquad(\alpha\beta\gamma)=(123),(231),(312). (3.32)

In the explicit form, this reads:

ϕ1​(a1​ϕ13−a2​ϕ23)​(a2​ϕ2−a3​ϕ3)ϕ3​(a2​ϕ12−a3​ϕ13)​(a1​ϕ1−a2​ϕ2)=1,\frac{\phi^{1}(a_{1}\phi^{13}-a_{2}\phi^{23})(a_{2}\phi^{2}-a_{3}\phi^{3})}{\phi^{3}(a_{2}\phi^{12}-a_{3}\phi^{13})(a_{1}\phi^{1}-a_{2}\phi^{2})}=1, (3.33)

which is equivalent to the similar equations obtained from it by cyclic permutations of the indices 1,2,31,2,3.

So far we were following the way from KP to mKP. The next theorem (inverse to Theorem 3.2) shows that there is also a way back: starting from a solution to equation (3.27) (or (3.29)) it is possible to restore the corresponding solutions τ\tau, τ^\hat{\tau} to the KP hierarchy.

Theorem 3.3

Let ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) be any solution of the mKP equation (3.29) (or (3.33)). Then there exist functions τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) and τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) such that both of them are KP tau-functions connected by equation (3.5).

In the proof, the following technical lemma is used.

Lemma 3.1

Let h⁡(𝐭,z)h({\bf t},z) be a function of 𝐭{\bf t}, zz satisfying the functional relation

h⁡(𝐭−[a−1],b)h⁡(𝐭,b)=h⁡(𝐭−[b−1],a)h⁡(𝐭,a)\frac{h({\bf t}-[a^{-1}],b)}{h({\bf t},b)}=\frac{h({\bf t}-[b^{-1}],a)}{h({\bf t},a)}

for all a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mbox{\Bbb C}. Then there exists a function H⁡(𝐭)H({\bf t}) such that

h⁡(𝐭,a)=H⁡(𝐭−[a−1])H⁡(𝐭).h({\bf t},a)=\frac{H({\bf t}-[a^{-1}])}{H({\bf t})}.

A detailed proof of this lemma can be found in [4].

R⁡(𝐭,a,b)=a​ϕ​(𝐭−[a−1])−b​ϕ​(𝐭−[b−1])ϕ⁡(𝐭),R({\bf t},a,b)=\frac{a\phi({\bf t}-[a^{-1}])-b\phi({\bf t}-[b^{-1}])}{\phi({\bf t})}, (3.34)

which shows that F^\hat{F} can be identified with the KP tau-function τ^\hat{\tau} satisfying equation (3.7) (and, therefore, (3.5)).  

The following proposition will be used in Section 4.2.

Proposition 3.2

Let ϕ\phi and ϕ′\phi^{\prime} be any two different solutions to the mKP hierarchy (i.e., solutions to (3.29)). Then any linear combination ϕ′′=a​ϕ+b​ϕ′\phi^{\prime\prime}=a\phi+b\phi^{\prime} with a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mbox{\Bbb C} is a solution to the mKP hierarchy if and only if ϕ\phi and ϕ′\phi^{\prime} are wave functions corresponding to the same solution of the KP hierarchy.

where ϕ′′=a​ϕ+b​ϕ′\phi^{\prime\prime}=a\phi+b\phi^{\prime} and

holds together with the same equations for u′u^{\prime} and u′′u^{\prime\prime}. Subtracting the last equation in (3.39) from the sum of the first two, we get:

To overcome this difficulty, we proceed as follows. Equation (3.41) can be rewritten as

(3.42)
