3.3 Baker-Akhiezer functions for the mKP hierarchy

Just as it was done for the KP hierarchy, one may introduce BA functions for the mKP hierarchy, so that they would satisfy a bilinear relation similar to (2.13). Following [31, 32, 14], we define them by the formulas

φ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])τ^​(𝐭),φ∗​(𝐭,z)=e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ^​(𝐭+[z−1])z​τ​(𝐭).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\varphi({\bf t},z)=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})}},\\ \\ \displaystyle{\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\frac{\hat{\tau}({\bf t}+[z^{-1}])}{z\,\tau({\bf t})}}.\end{array} (3.43)

They are connected with the BA functions for the KP hierarchy in the following way:

φ⁡(𝐭,z)=ϕ−1​(𝐭)​ψ​(𝐭,z),φ∗​(𝐭,z)=ϕ⁡(𝐭)​ψ^∗​(𝐭,z).\begin{array}[]{l}\varphi({\bf t},z)=\phi^{-1}({\bf t})\psi({\bf t},z),\\ \\ \varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=\phi({\bf t})\hat{\psi}^{*}({\bf t},z).\end{array} (3.44)

The expansions as z→∞z\to\infty are of the form

φ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​(w0​(𝐭)+w1​(𝐭)​z−1+w2​(𝐭)​z−2+…),φ∗​(𝐭,z)=z−1​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z)​(w0−1​(𝐭)+w1∗​(𝐭)​z−1+w2∗​(𝐭)​z−2+…),\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\varphi({\bf t},z)=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\Bigl(w_{0}({\bf t})+w_{1}({\bf t})z^{-1}+w_{2}({\bf t})z^{-2}+\ldots\,\Bigr),}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=z^{-1}e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}\,\Bigl(w_{0}^{-1}({\bf t})+w^{*}_{1}({\bf t})z^{-1}+w^{*}_{2}({\bf t})z^{-2}+\ldots\,\Bigr),}\end{array} (3.45)

where

w0​(𝐭)=τ⁡(𝐭)τ^​(𝐭)=(ϕ⁡(𝐭))−1w_{0}({\bf t})=\frac{\tau({\bf t})}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})}=(\phi({\bf t}))^{-1}\, (3.46)

(see (3.12)). In terms of the φ\varphi-functions, equation (3.5) acquires the form

12​π​i​∮C∞φ⁡(𝐭,z)​φ∗​(𝐭′,z)​𝑑z=1.\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{C_{\infty}}\!\varphi({\bf t},z)\varphi^{*}({\bf t^{\prime}},z)\,dz=1. (3.47)

Its role in the mKP theory is the same as that of equation (2.13) for the KP theory (see Remark 2.1).

3.4 Lax-Sato formalism for the mKP hierarchy

One can introduce an mKP-analogue of the dressing operator. It is a pseudo-differential operator 𝒲{\cal W} of order 0 of the form

𝒲=w0+w1∂x−1+w2∂x−2+…,{\cal W}=w_{0}+w_{1}\partial_{x}^{-1}+w_{2}\partial_{x}^{-2}+\ldots\,, (3.48)

where the coefficient functions wi=wi​(𝐭)w_{i}=w_{i}({\bf t}) are the same as in (3.45). Clearly, we can write

φ⁡(𝐭,z)=𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z).\varphi({\bf t},z)={\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}. (3.49)

The Lax operator for the mKP hierarchy is defined as

ℒ=𝒲∂x𝒲−1=∂x+v0+v1∂x−1+v2∂x−2+…,{\cal L}={\cal W}\partial_{x}{\cal W}^{-1}=\partial_{x}+v_{0}+v_{1}\partial_{x}^{-1}+v_{2}\partial_{x}^{-2}+\ldots\,, (3.50)

where

v0=−∂xlogw0.v_{0}=-\partial_{x}\log w_{0}. (3.51)

It is a pseudo-differential operator of order 1, but, unlike the Lax operator for KP, the coefficient in front of (∂x)0(\partial_{x})^{0} is nonzero. Along with the Lax operator, we introduce the purely differential operators

ℬk=(ℒk)≥1,k≥1.{\cal B}_{k}=({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1},\qquad k\geq 1. (3.52)

For example, ℬ1=∂x{\cal B}_{1}=\partial_{x}, ℬ2=∂x2+v0∂x{\cal B}_{2}=\partial_{x}^{2}+v_{0}\partial_{x}.

The next theorem is an mKP-analogue of Theorem 2.1.

Theorem 3.4

Let φ⁡(𝐭,z)\varphi({\bf t},z), φ∗​(𝐭,z)\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z) be functions of the form (3.45). If the bilinear relation (3.47) is satisfied, then there exists a dressing operator 𝒲{\cal W} of the form (3.48) such that φ⁡(𝐭,z)=𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)\varphi({\bf t},z)={\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)} satisfying the evolution equations

∂tk𝒲=−(ℒk)≤0​𝒲​for any k≥1.\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal W}=-({\cal L}^{k})_{\leq 0}{\cal W}\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}. (3.53)

Proof. For the proof we need the following mKP-analogue of Lemma 2.1:

Lemma 3.2

Let 𝒫{\cal P} and 𝒬{\cal Q} be pseudo-differential operators of the form

𝒫=w(x)+∑j≥1pj(x)∂x−j,𝒬=w−1(x)(−∂x−1)+∑j≥1qj(x)(−∂x)−j−1.{\cal P}=w(x)+\sum_{j\geq 1}p_{j}(x)\partial_{x}^{-j},\quad{\cal Q}=w^{-1}(x)(-\partial_{x}^{-1})+\sum_{j\geq 1}q_{j}(x)(-\partial_{x})^{-j-1}.

Then the condition

∮C∞(𝒫x​ex​z)​(𝒬x′​e−x′​z)​𝑑z=c\oint_{C_{\infty}}({\cal P}_{x}e^{xz})\,({\cal Q}_{x^{\prime}}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=c (3.54)

for all x,x′x,x^{\prime}, where cc is some constant, implies that

(𝒫𝒬†)<0=c∂x−1.\Bigl({\cal P}\,{\cal Q}^{{\dagger}}\Bigr)_{<0}=c\partial_{x}^{-1}. (3.55)

Set

φ⁡(𝐭,z)=𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z),φ∗​(𝐭,z)=𝒱​e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z),\varphi({\bf t},z)={\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)},\quad\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)={\cal V}e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)},

where both 𝒲{\cal W} and 𝒱{\cal V} are of the form (3.48) (the latter one is of order −1-1). Plugging this into (3.47) with tk=tk′t_{k}=t^{\prime}_{k} for k≥2k\geq 2, we have:

∮C∞(𝒲x​ex​z)​(𝒱x′​e−x′​z)​𝑑z=1.\oint_{C_{\infty}}({\cal W}_{x}e^{xz})\,({\cal V}_{x^{\prime}}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=1.

Now we can apply Lemma 3.2 with 𝒫=𝒲{\cal P}={\cal W}, 𝒬=𝒱{\cal Q}={\cal V} and conclude that (𝒲𝒱†)<0=∂x−1({\cal W}\,{\cal V}^{{\dagger}})_{<0}=\partial_{x}^{-1}. Since the operator in the left-hand side is of negative order, we have 𝒲𝒱†=∂x−1{\cal W}\,{\cal V}^{{\dagger}}=\partial_{x}^{-1}, hence 𝒱=(𝒲−1∂x−1)†{\cal V}=({\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})^{{\dagger}} and φ∗(𝐭,z)=(𝒲−1∂x−1)†e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z).\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=({\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})^{{\dagger}}e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}.

Next, define the operators ℒ{\cal L} and ℬk{\cal B}_{k} as in (3.50) and (3.52). Then (3.47) implies

∮C∞(∂tn−ℬn)φ(𝐭,z)φ∗(𝐭′,z)dz=0\oint_{C_{\infty}}(\partial_{t_{n}}-{\cal B}_{n})\,\varphi({\bf t},z)\varphi^{*}({\bf t^{\prime}},z)\,dz=0 (3.56)

for all 𝐭{\bf t}, 𝐭′{\bf t^{\prime}}. We have, using (3.49) and (3.50):

(∂tn−ℬn)φ(𝐭,z)=(∂tn𝒲+𝒲∂xn−ℬn𝒲)eξ⁡(𝐭,z)(\partial_{t_{n}}-{\cal B}_{n})\varphi({\bf t},z)=(\partial_{t_{n}}{\cal W}+{\cal W}\partial_{x}^{n}-{\cal B}_{n}{\cal W})e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}
=(∂tn𝒲+ℒn​𝒲−ℬn​𝒲)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(∂tn𝒲+(ℒn)≤0​𝒲)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z).=(\partial_{t_{n}}{\cal W}+{\cal L}^{n}{\cal W}-{\cal B}_{n}{\cal W})e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=(\partial_{t_{n}}{\cal W}+({\cal L}^{n})_{\leq 0}{\cal W})e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}.

Again, putting tk=tk′t_{k}=t_{k}^{\prime} for k≥2k\geq 2, we rewrite (3.56) as

∮C∞(ℛex​z)((𝒲−1∂x−1)†e−x′​z)dz=0,\oint_{C_{\infty}}({\cal R}e^{xz})\,(({\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})^{{\dagger}}e^{-x^{\prime}z})\,dz=0,

where ℛ{\cal R} is the operator ℛ=∂tn𝒲+(ℒn)≤0​𝒲{\cal R}=\partial_{t_{n}}{\cal W}+({\cal L}^{n})_{\leq 0}{\cal W}. By Lemma 3.2 (with c=0c=0), we conclude that (ℛ𝒲−1∂x−1)<0=0({\cal R}\,{\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})_{<0}=0. Clearly, ℛ{\cal R} contains non-positive powers of ∂x\partial_{x} only while the operator ℛ𝒲−1∂x−1{\cal R}\,{\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1} is of strictly negative order i.e., (ℛ𝒲−1∂x−1)≤0=ℛ𝒲−1∂x−1=0({\cal R}\,{\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})_{\leq 0}={\cal R}\,{\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1}=0. Since 𝒲{\cal W} is an invertible operator of order zero, it follows from this that ℛ=0{\cal R}=0, which proves (3.53).  

Corollary 3.1

The function φ⁡(𝐭,z)\varphi({\bf t},z) is an eigenfunction of the Lax operator ℒ{\cal L} (3.50) with eigenvalue zz,

ℒ​φ​(𝐭,z)=z​φ​(𝐭,z),{\cal L}\varphi({\bf t},z)=z\varphi({\bf t},z), (3.57)

and for any z∈ℂz\in\mbox{\Bbb C} it satisfies the differential equations

∂tkφ⁡(𝐭,z)=ℬk​φ​(𝐭,z)​for any k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi({\bf t},z)={\cal B}_{k}\varphi({\bf t},z)\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (3.58)

where the kk-th order differential operators ℬk{\cal B}_{k} of the form ℬk=∂xk+∑j=1k−1ck∂xj\displaystyle{{\cal B}_{k}=\partial_{x}^{k}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}c_{k}\partial_{x}^{j}} are given by equation (3.52).

Proof. The eigenvalue equation (3.57) is a trivial consequence of (3.49), (3.50). Equation (3.58) easily follows from (3.53):

∂tkφ⁡(𝐭,z)=∂tk𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)+𝒲​zk​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=−(ℒk)≤0​𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)+𝒲​∂xkeξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(−(ℒk)≤0+ℒk)​𝒲​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=(ℒk)≥1​φ​(𝐭,z).\begin{array}[]{lll}\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi({\bf t},z)&=&\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal W}\,e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}+{\cal W}z^{k}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\\ &&\\ &=&-({\cal L}^{k})_{\leq 0}{\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}+{\cal W}\partial_{x}^{k}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\\ &&\\ &=&\Bigl(-({\cal L}^{k})_{\leq 0}+{\cal L}^{k}\Bigr){\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}\varphi({\bf t},z).\end{array}
 

There are similar statements for the adjoint BA function φ∗​(𝐭,z)\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z). From the proof of Theorem 3.4 we already know that

φ∗(𝐭,z)=(𝒲−1∂x−1)†e−ξ⁡(𝐭,z).\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=({\cal W}^{-1}\partial_{x}^{-1})^{{\dagger}}e^{-\xi({\bf t},z)}. (3.59)

Using (3.53) one can prove the following corollary.

Corollary 3.2

The function φ∗​(𝐭,z)\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z) satisfies the equations

ℒ∗​φ∗​(𝐭,z)=z​φ∗​(𝐭,z),{\cal L}^{*}\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)=z\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z), (3.60)
−∂tkφ∗(𝐭,z)=ℬ∗φ∗(𝐭,z)for any k≥1,-\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)={\cal B}^{*}\varphi^{*}({\bf t},z)\;\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (3.61)

where

ℒ∗=∂x−1ℒ†k∂x,ℬ∗=∂x−1ℬ†k∂x.{\cal L}^{*}=\partial_{x}^{-1}{\cal L}^{{\dagger}}_{k}\,\partial_{x},\qquad{\cal B}^{*}=\partial_{x}^{-1}{\cal B}^{{\dagger}}_{k}\,\partial_{x}. (3.62)
Remark 3.3

Taking into account equations (2.11), we can represent the dressing operator 𝒲{\cal W} as

𝒲=∙∙​τ(𝐭−[∂x−1])τ^​(𝐭)​∙∙,(𝒲†)−1=∙∙​τ^(𝐭+[∂x−1])τ⁡(𝐭)​∙∙{\cal W}={\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}}\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})}{\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}},\qquad({\cal W}^{{\dagger}})^{-1}={\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}}\frac{\hat{\tau}({\bf t}+[\partial_{x}^{-1}])}{\tau({\bf t})}{\scriptstyle{{\bullet}\atop{\bullet}}} (3.63)

where the normal ordering means that operator ∂x\partial_{x} in each term of the expansion in negative powers of ∂x−1\partial_{x}^{-1} is moved to the right. (cf. Remark 2.3).

Like in the case of the KP hierarchy, compatibility of equations (3.57), (3.58) implies the Lax equations

∂tkℒ=[ℬk,ℒ],k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal L}=[{\cal B}_{k},{\cal L}],\quad k\geq 1, (3.64)

and equations of the Zakharov-Shabat type

∂tnℬm−∂tmℬn+[ℬm,ℬn]=0,n,m≥1.\partial_{t_{n}}{\cal B}_{m}-\partial_{t_{m}}{\cal B}_{n}+[{\cal B}_{m},{\cal B}_{n}]=0,\quad n,m\geq 1. (3.65)

Usually, this infinite system of equations serves as a definition of the mKP hierarchy.

Wave functions for the mKP hierarchy are introduced in the same way as in the KP case (see Definition 2.1).

Definition 3.1

Any solution S⁡(𝐭)S({\bf t}) to the system of linear differential equations (3.58), i.e.,

∂tkS⁡(𝐭)=ℬk​S​(𝐭)for any k≥1,\partial_{t_{k}}S({\bf t})={\cal B}_{k}S({\bf t})\;\;\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (3.66)

is called a wave function for the mKP hierarchy. Any solution S∗​(𝐭)S^{*}({\bf t}) to the system (3.61), i.e.,

−∂tkS∗(𝐭)=ℬ∗kS∗(𝐭)for any k≥1,-\partial_{t_{k}}S^{*}({\bf t})={\cal B^{*}}_{k}S^{*}({\bf t})\;\;\;\;\mbox{for any $k\geq 1$}, (3.67)

is called an adjoint wave function.

For brevity, we will sometimes call both SS and S∗S^{*} wave functions.

Like in the KP case, mKP wave functions of general form can be obtained by integrating the mKP BA functions with respect to the spectral parameter zz with arbitrary density functions or distributions σ⁡(z)\sigma(z), σ∗​(z)\sigma^{*}(z):

S⁡(𝐭)=∫ℂφ⁡(𝐭,z)​σ​(z)​d2​z,S∗​(𝐭)=∫ℂφ∗​(𝐭,z)​σ∗​(z)​d2​z.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{S({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\varphi({\bf t};z)\sigma(z)d^{2}z,}\\ \\ \displaystyle{S^{*}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\varphi^{*}({\bf t};z)\sigma^{*}(z)d^{2}z}.\end{array} (3.68)
Remark 3.4

Since the operators ℬk{\cal B}_{k}, ℬ^k\hat{\cal B}_{k} are of the form 𝒜∂x{\cal A}\,\partial_{x}, where 𝒜{\cal A} is a differential operator, the simplest mKP wave functions are S⁡(𝐭)=S∗​(𝐭)=1S({\bf t})=S^{*}({\bf t})=1.

4 From mKP to SchKP (and HD) and back

4.1 BD transformations of the mKP hierarchy

In the previous section the mKP hierarchy was described in terms of a BD transformation of KP. Such a BD transformation of any solution τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) of the KP hierarchy to another solution τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) is determined by choosing a wave function ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}) of the KP hierarchy, then τ^​(𝐭)=ϕ​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\phi({\bf t})\tau({\bf t}). The pair (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) obtained in this way is a solution of the mKP hierarchy.

A similar description of the SchKP and HD hierarchies requires that in addition to the already selected KP wave function ϕ\phi, one should fix another one, ϕ′​(𝐭)\phi^{\prime}({\bf t}). This wave function defines another BD transformation τ→τ¯=ϕ′​τ\tau\to\bar{\tau}=\phi^{\prime}\tau for KP, and thus the pair (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) is some other solution to the mKP hierarchy. The transition from (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) to (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) is nothing else than a BD transformation for the mKP hierarchy. Alternatively (and equivalently) it can be described in the same manner as it was done for the KP hierarchy: given a solution (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}), we construct another solution by fixing a wave function S⁡(𝐭)S({\bf t}) of the mKP hierarchy, then τ¯=S​τ\bar{\tau}=S\tau, with S=ϕ′/ϕS=\phi^{\prime}/\phi.

As a preliminary step, we should obtain a bilinear equation which connects the tau-functions τ\tau, τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau}. To this end, we need to consider composition of the KP BD transformations τ→τ^\tau\to\hat{\tau} and τ→τ¯\tau\to\bar{\tau} which sends τ\tau to some other KP tau-function which we denote as τ¯^\hat{\bar{\tau}}. It is instructive to define it in a slightly more general setup. Consider two chains of forward BD transformations defined by fixing two sequences of density functions {ρ1(1)​(z),ρ2(1)​(z),…}\{\rho_{1}^{(1)}(z),\rho_{2}^{(1)}(z),\ldots\} and {ρ1(2)​(z),ρ2(2)​(z),…}\{\rho_{1}^{(2)}(z),\rho_{2}^{(2)}(z),\ldots\}. Starting from any initial KP tau-function τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}), one can apply the first transformation n1n_{1} times and then the second one n2n_{2} times. We denote the resulting tau-function as τ⁡(n1,n2,𝐭)\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t}). Let us denote the first and the second transformations by 𝐁1{\bf B}_{1} and 𝐁2{\bf B}_{2}, then we can write:

𝐁1​τ​(n1,n2,𝐭)=τ⁡(n1+1,n2,𝐭)=∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,z)​zn1+n2​ρn1+1(1)​(z)​τ​(n1,n2,𝐭−[z−1])​d2​z,𝐁2​τ​(n1,n2,𝐭)=τ⁡(n1,n2+1,𝐭)=∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,z)​zn1+n2​ρn2+1(2)​(z)​τ​(n1,n2,𝐭−[z−1])​d2​z.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{{\bf B}_{1}\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t})=\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2},{\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}z^{n_{1}+n_{2}}\rho^{(1)}_{n_{1}+1}(z)\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])d^{2}z,}\\ \\ \displaystyle{{\bf B}_{2}\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t})=\tau(n_{1},n_{2}+1,{\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}z^{n_{1}+n_{2}}\rho^{(2)}_{n_{2}+1}(z)\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}])d^{2}z.}\end{array} (4.1)

There are two ways to obtain τ⁡(n1+1,n2+1,𝐭)\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2}+1,{\bf t}) from τ⁡(n1,n2,𝐭)\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t}) (first apply 𝐁1{\bf B}_{1}, then 𝐁2{\bf B}_{2} or vice versa):

τ⁡(n1,n2,𝐭)⟶𝐁1τ⁡(n1+1,n2,𝐭)⟶𝐁2τ⁡(n1+1,n2+1,𝐭),\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\bf B}_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2},{\bf t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\bf B}_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2}+1,{\bf t}),
τ⁡(n1,n2,𝐭)⟶𝐁2τ⁡(n1,n2+1,𝐭)⟶𝐁1τ⁡(n1+1,n2+1,𝐭).\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\bf B}_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\tau(n_{1},n_{2}+1,{\bf t})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\bf B}_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2}+1,{\bf t}).

Writing the two composite transformations explicitly as double integrals, one can easily see that the results differ by a sign, i.e., the anti-commutation relation

𝐁1​𝐁2=−𝐁2​𝐁1{\bf B}_{1}{\bf B}_{2}=-{\bf B}_{2}{\bf B}_{1} (4.2)

holds true. Therefore, given τ⁡(n1,n2,𝐭)\tau(n_{1},n_{2},{\bf t}), the function τ⁡(n1+1,n2+1,𝐭)\tau(n_{1}+1,n_{2}+1,{\bf t}) is defined only up to a sign. For our needs, it is enough to fix this uncertainty by the convention that the transformation τ→τ^\tau\to\hat{\tau} (which is 𝐁1{\bf B}_{1}) is applied first. So, we have four KP tau-functions

τ⁡(𝐭)=τ⁡(0,0,𝐭),τ^​(𝐭)=τ⁡(1,0,𝐭),τ¯​(𝐭)=τ⁡(0,1,𝐭),τ¯^​(𝐭)=τ⁡(1,1,𝐭).\tau({\bf t})=\tau(0,0,{\bf t}),\quad\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\tau(1,0,{\bf t}),\quad\bar{\tau}({\bf t})=\tau(0,1,{\bf t}),\quad\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t})=\tau(1,1,{\bf t}). (4.3)
Proposition 4.1

The four KP tau-functions (4.3) satisfy the bilinear equation

a⁡(τ^​(𝐭−[a−1])​τ¯​(𝐭)−τ¯​(𝐭−[a−1])​τ^​(𝐭))=τ¯^​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭−[a−1]),a\Bigl(\hat{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}-[a^{-1}]\bigr)\bar{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}\bigr)-\bar{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}-[a^{-1}]\bigr)\hat{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}\bigr)\Bigr)=\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t}\bigr)\,\tau({\bf t}-[a^{-1}]\bigr), (4.4)

or, in the short-hand notation,

a1​(τ^1​τ¯−τ¯1​τ^)=τ¯^​τ1.a_{1}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{1}\bar{\tau}-\bar{\tau}^{1}\hat{\tau}\Bigr)=\hat{\bar{\tau}}\,\tau^{1}. (4.5)

Proof. Explicitly, the tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau}, τ¯\bar{\tau} and τ¯^\hat{\bar{\tau}} are given by

τ^​(𝐭)=∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,z)​ρ^​(z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1])​d2​z,τ¯​(𝐭)=∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,w)​ρ¯​(w)​τ​(𝐭−[w−1])​d2​w,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\hat{\rho}(z)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]\Bigr)d^{2}z,}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\bar{\tau}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},w)}\bar{\rho}(w)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[w^{-1}]\Bigr)d^{2}w,}\end{array}
τ¯^​(𝐭)=∫ℂ∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,z)+ξ⁡(𝐭,w)​ρ^​(z)​ρ¯​(w)​(w−z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1]−[w−1])​d2​z​d2​w.\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t})=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\!\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)+\xi({\bf t},w)}\hat{\rho}(z)\bar{\rho}(w)(w-z)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]-[w^{-1}]\Bigr)d^{2}zd^{2}w.

Using these formulas, we can write:

a1​(τ^​(𝐭−[a1−1])​τ¯​(𝐭)−τ¯​(𝐭−[a1−1])​τ^​(𝐭))−τ¯^​(𝐭)​τ​(𝐭−[a−1])=∫ℂ∫ℂeξ⁡(𝐭,z)+ξ⁡(𝐭,w)​ρ^​(z)​ρ¯​(w)​T​(z,w,𝐭)​d2​z​d2​w,\begin{array}[]{l}a_{1}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]\bigr)\bar{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}\bigr)-\bar{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]\bigr)\hat{\tau}\bigl({\bf t}\bigr)\Bigr)-\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t}\bigr)\,\tau({\bf t}-[a^{-1}]\bigr)\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\displaystyle{=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\!\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)+\xi({\bf t},w)}\hat{\rho}(z)\bar{\rho}(w)\,T(z,w,{\bf t})d^{2}zd^{2}w,}\end{array} (4.6)

where

T⁡(z,w,𝐭)=(a1−z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1]−[a1−1])​τ​(𝐭−[w−1])−(a1−w)​τ​(𝐭−[w−1]−[a1−1])​τ​(𝐭−[z−1])−(w−z)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1]−[w−1])​τ​(𝐭−[a1−1]).\begin{array}[]{lll}T(z,w,{\bf t})&=&(a_{1}-z)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]-[a_{1}^{-1}]\Bigr)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[w^{-1}]\Bigr)\\ &&\\ &&-(a_{1}-w)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[w^{-1}]-[a_{1}^{-1}]\Bigr)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]\Bigr)\\ &&\\ &&-(w-z)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]-[w^{-1}]\Bigr)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}-[a_{1}^{-1}]\Bigr).\end{array}

But since τ⁡(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}) is a KP tau-function, T⁡(z,w,𝐭)=0T(z,w,{\bf t})=0 by virtue of equation (2.2), where one should put a2=za_{2}=z, a3=wa_{3}=w.  

We will need two corollaries of equation (4.5) obtained by expanding the both sides in inverse powers of a1a_{1} as a1→∞a_{1}\to\infty. In the leading order we obtain the equation

∂xlog⁡τ¯τ^=τ¯^​ττ^​τ¯\partial_{x}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}=\frac{\hat{\bar{\tau}}\,\tau}{\hat{\tau}\,\bar{\tau}} (4.7)

(recall that x=t1x=t_{1}). The expansion to the next order gives the equation

∂t2log⁡τ¯τ^−∂x2log⁡τ¯τ^+(∂xlog⁡τ^)2−(∂xlog⁡τ¯)2+2​τ¯^​ττ^​τ¯​∂xlog⁡τ=0.\partial_{t_{2}}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}-\partial^{2}_{x}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}+(\partial_{x}\log\hat{\tau})^{2}-(\partial_{x}\log\bar{\tau})^{2}+2\frac{\hat{\bar{\tau}}\,\tau}{\hat{\tau}\,\bar{\tau}}\,\partial_{x}\log\tau=0. (4.8)

Combining it with (4.7), one can exclude τ¯^\hat{\bar{\tau}} and obtain the equation

∂t2log⁡τ¯τ^−∂x2log⁡τ¯τ^−(∂xlog⁡τ¯τ^)2−2​(∂xlog⁡τ^τ)​(∂xlog⁡τ¯τ^)=0,\partial_{t_{2}}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}-\partial^{2}_{x}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}-\Bigl(\partial_{x}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}\Bigr)^{2}-2\Bigl(\partial_{x}\log\frac{\hat{\tau}}{\tau}\Bigr)\Bigl(\partial_{x}\log\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\hat{\tau}}\Bigr)=0, (4.9)

which will be used below.

It is convenient to depict the four KP tau-functions (4.3) on the following diagram:

τ¯⟶ϕ¯τ¯^↑ϕ′↑ϕ^τ⟶ϕτ^\begin{array}[]{ccc}\bar{\tau}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bar{\phi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\bar{\tau}}\\ \uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle\phi^{\prime}}$\hss}&&\uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle\hat{\phi}}$\hss}\\ \tau&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\tau}\end{array} (4.10)

Each arrow in (4.10) is equipped with the KP wave function that defines the corresponding mKP solution (i.e., the KP BD transformation). They are:

ϕ=τ^τ,ϕ′=τ¯τ,ϕ¯=τ¯^τ¯,ϕ^=τ¯^τ^.\phi=\frac{\hat{\tau}}{\tau},\quad\phi^{\prime}=\frac{\bar{\tau}}{\tau},\quad\bar{\phi}=\frac{\hat{\bar{\tau}}}{\bar{\tau}},\quad\hat{\phi}=\frac{\hat{\bar{\tau}}}{\hat{\tau}}. (4.11)

The first two are associated with the KP Lax operator LL corresponding to the initial solution with the tau-function τ\tau, while the other two, ϕ¯\bar{\phi} and ϕ^\hat{\phi}, are associated with the KP Lax operators L¯\bar{L} and L^\hat{L} corresponding to the KP solutions with the tau-functions τ¯\bar{\tau} and τ^\hat{\tau} respectively. The mKP Lax operators for the four mKP solutions (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}), (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}), (τ^,τ¯^)(\hat{\tau},\hat{\bar{\tau}}), (τ¯,τ¯^)(\bar{\tau},\hat{\bar{\tau}}) will be denoted as ℒ{\cal L}, ℒ′{\cal L}^{\prime}, ℒ^\hat{\cal L}, ℒ¯\bar{\cal L} respectively. Each of them is obtained by “dressing” the differential operator ∂x\partial_{x} with the dressing operators 𝒲{\cal W}, 𝒲′{\cal W}^{\prime}, 𝒲^\hat{\cal W}, 𝒲¯\bar{\cal W} as in (3.50):

τ¯⟶𝒲¯τ¯^↑𝒲′↑𝒲^τ⟶𝒲τ^\begin{array}[]{ccc}\bar{\tau}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bar{\cal W}}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\bar{\tau}}\\ \uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle{\cal W}^{\prime}}$\hss}&&\uparrow\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\scriptstyle\hat{\cal W}}$\hss}\\ \tau&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\cal W}}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\hat{\tau}\end{array} (4.12)

Accordingly, along with φ⁡(𝐭,z)\varphi({\bf t},z) given by (3.43), we can introduce the BA functions for the other three solutions:

φ′​(𝐭,z)=𝒲′​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])τ¯​(𝐭),φ^​(𝐭,z)=𝒲^​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ^​(𝐭−[z−1])τ¯^​(𝐭),φ¯​(𝐭,z)=𝒲¯​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)=eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ¯​(𝐭−[z−1])τ¯^​(𝐭).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\varphi^{\prime}({\bf t},z)={\cal W}^{\prime}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\frac{\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\bar{\tau}({\bf t})}},\\ \\ \displaystyle{\hat{\varphi}({\bf t},z)=\hat{\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\frac{\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t})}},\\ \\ \displaystyle{\bar{\varphi}({\bf t},z)=\bar{\cal W}e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}=e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\frac{\bar{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t})}}.\end{array} (4.13)

The next theorem states that the mKP dressing operators 𝒲′{\cal W}^{\prime}, 𝒲^\hat{\cal W}, 𝒲¯\bar{\cal W} can be expressed through 𝒲{\cal W} and the ratio

S⁡(𝐭)=τ¯​(𝐭)τ^​(𝐭),S({\bf t})=\frac{\bar{\tau}({\bf t})}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})}, (4.14)

which in what follows will be identified with a wave function for the mKP Lax operator ℒ{\cal L} in the sense of Definition 3.1 (see Theorem 4.4 below).

Theorem 4.1

The dressing operators 𝒲′{\cal W}^{\prime}, 𝒲^\hat{\cal W}, 𝒲¯\bar{\cal W} in the diagram (4.12) are expressed through 𝒲{\cal W} and SS given by (4.14) as follows:

𝒲′=S−1​𝒲,𝒲^=Sx−1∂x𝒲∂x−1,𝒲¯=Sx−1S2∂xS−1𝒲∂x−1,\begin{array}[]{l}{\cal W}^{\prime}=S^{-1}{\cal W},\\ \\ \hat{\cal W}=S_{x}^{-1}\partial_{x}{\cal W}\partial_{x}^{-1},\\ \\ \bar{\cal W}=S_{x}^{-1}S^{2}\partial_{x}S^{-1}{\cal W}\partial_{x}^{-1},\end{array} (4.15)

where the right-hand sides are to be understood as compositions of the operators and Sx=∂xSS_{x}=\partial_{x}S.

Proof. The first equality in (4.15) is evident from the definitions. To prove the second one, it is enough to check the equality

eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​τ^​(𝐭−[z−1])τ¯^​(𝐭)=z−1​Sx−1​(𝐭)​∂xφ⁡(𝐭,z)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\frac{\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t})}=z^{-1}S_{x}^{-1}({\bf t})\partial_{x}\varphi({\bf t},z) (4.16)

which is the result of acting by both sides of 𝒲^=Sx−1∂x𝒲∂x−1\hat{\cal W}=S_{x}^{-1}\partial_{x}{\cal W}\partial_{x}^{-1} to the exponential function eξ⁡(𝐭,z)e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}. Plugging here φ\varphi from (3.43), we rewrite (4.16) as

Sx​τ^[z]τ¯^=τ[z]τ^​(1+z−1​∂xlog⁡τ[z]τ^),S_{x}\,\frac{\hat{\tau}^{[z]}}{\hat{\bar{\tau}}}=\frac{\tau^{[z]}}{\hat{\tau}}\Bigl(1+z^{-1}\partial_{x}\log\frac{\tau^{[z]}}{\hat{\tau}}\Bigr), (4.17)

where for the sake of brevity we have denoted τ[z]=τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1])\tau^{[z]}=\tau({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]), τ^[z]=τ^​(𝐭−[z−1])\hat{\tau}^{[z]}=\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}]). Equation (4.7) states that

Sx=τ¯^​ττ^2,S_{x}=\frac{\hat{\bar{\tau}}\tau}{\hat{\tau}^{2}}, (4.18)

which is to be substituted into the the left-hand side of (4.17). To transform the right-hand side, we use equation (3.7). Letting a2→∞a_{2}\to\infty and a1=za_{1}=z in it, we obtain the equality

1+z−1​∂xlog⁡τ[z]τ^=τ^[z]​ττ^​τ[z],1+z^{-1}\partial_{x}\log\frac{\tau^{[z]}}{\hat{\tau}}=\frac{\hat{\tau}^{[z]}\tau}{\hat{\tau}\tau^{[z]}},

which, together with (4.18), converts equation (4.17) into identity. The third equation in (4.15) can be proved in a similar way.  

Remark 4.1

The BD transformations of the mKP hierarchy defined by the diagram (4.10) were considered in [12, 32] (along with transformations of some other types) under the name of “gauge transformations”.

4.2 From mKP to SchKP and back

The pair of KP tau-functions (τ^,τ¯)(\hat{\tau},\bar{\tau}) considered in Section 4.1 can be regarded as a solution of the SchKP and, after a change of variables, HD hierarchies. Moreover, any solution of the latter hierarchies can be obtained in this way.

It turns out that there exist bilinear equations which connect τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau}, without any participation of τ\tau.

Theorem 4.2

Let the pairs (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}), (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) be any two solutions of the mKP hierarchy with the same first members of the pairs. Then the KP tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau}, τ¯\bar{\tau} satisfy the bilinear equation

∮C∞eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,λ)​[τ^​(𝐭−[λ−1])​τ¯​(𝐭′+[λ−1])+τ^​(𝐭′+[λ−1])​τ¯​(𝐭−[λ−1])]​𝑑λ=0\oint_{C_{\infty}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}},\lambda)}\Bigl[\hat{\tau}({\bf t}-[\lambda^{-1}])\bar{\tau}({\bf t^{\prime}}+[\lambda^{-1}])+\hat{\tau}({\bf t^{\prime}}+[\lambda^{-1}])\bar{\tau}({\bf t}-[\lambda^{-1}])\Bigr]\,d\lambda=0 (4.19)

valid for all 𝐭,𝐭′{\bf t},\,{\bf t^{\prime}}.

Proof. The first step is to make the Miwa substitution (2.6) in (4.19), which converts the equation to be proved into the following one:

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​Δm​(a1,…,a^k,…,am+1)​∏i=1m−1(bi−ak)×[τ^(𝐭−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])τ¯(𝐭−[a−1k]−∑j=1m−1[bj−1])+τ¯(𝐭−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])τ^(𝐭−[a−1k]−∑j=1m−1[bj−1])]=0,m≥2.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\Delta_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{k},\ldots,a_{m+1})\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(b_{i}-a_{k})}\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaa}\displaystyle{\times\,\left[\hat{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\bar{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-[a^{-1}_{k}]-\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}[b_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\right.}\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\displaystyle{+\,\left.\bar{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\hat{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-[a^{-1}_{k}]-\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}[b_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\right]=0,\quad m\geq 2.}\end{array} (4.20)

(The residue calculus is the same as the one leading to (2.7).) In fact, equation (4.20) is actually equivalent to (4.19). Namely, the argument from [36] (see the proof of Proposition 1 there), which uses properties of symmetric functions, allows us to prove the following proposition.

Proposition 4.2

Equations (4.19) and (4.20) are equivalent (provided that the latter one is valid for all m≥2m\geq 2 and all sets of points).

Using the short-hand notation (2.3), we write:

τ^​(𝐭−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])=τ^1​…​k^​…​m+1,τ¯​(𝐭−[ak−1]−∑l=1m−1[bl−1])=τ¯k​1~​…​m−1~,\hat{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\!\!\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)=\hat{\tau}^{1\,\ldots\,\hat{k}\ldots\,m\!+\!1},\qquad\bar{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\![a_{k}^{-1}]-\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{m-1}[b_{l}^{-1}]\Bigr)=\bar{\tau}^{k\tilde{1}\,\ldots\,\widetilde{m\!-\!1}},

where l~\tilde{l} is related to blb_{l}. This allows us to represent (4.20) in a more compact form:

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1Δm(a1,…,a^k,…,am+1)Δm(ak,b1,…,,bm−1)×(τ^1​…​k^​…​m+1​τ¯k​1~​…​m−1~+τ¯1​…​k^​…​m+1​τ^k​1~​…​m−1~)=0.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\Delta_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{k},\ldots,a_{m+1})\Delta_{m}(a_{k},b_{1},\,\ldots,\,,b_{m-1})}\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\displaystyle{\times\,\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{1\,\ldots\,\hat{k}\ldots\,m\!+\!1}\,\bar{\tau}^{k\tilde{1}\,\ldots\,\widetilde{m\!-\!1}}\,+\,\bar{\tau}^{1\,\ldots\,\hat{k}\ldots\,m\!+\!1}\,\hat{\tau}^{k\tilde{1}\,\ldots\,\widetilde{m\!-\!1}}\Bigr)=0.}\end{array} (4.21)

The next step is to use the first equation in (2.36). Adopted to our case, it yields:

τ^​(𝐭−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])=∫ℂd2​z​ρ^​(z)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)​(∏j=1,≠km+1aj−zaj)​τ​(𝐭−[z−1]−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\hat{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\!\!\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}d^{2}z\hat{\rho}(z)\,e^{\xi({\bf t},z)}\Bigl(\prod_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}\!\!\frac{a_{j}-z}{a_{j}}\Bigr)\tau\Bigl({\bf t}\!-\![z^{-1}]-\!\!\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)}\end{array} (4.22)
τ¯​(𝐭−[ak−1]−∑l=1m−1[bl−1])=∫ℂd2​ζ​ρ¯​(ζ)​eξ⁡(𝐭,ζ)​ak−ζak​(∏j=1,≠km+1bl−ζbl)×τ⁡(𝐭−[ζ−1]−[ak−1]−∑l=1m−1[bl−1]).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\bar{\tau}\Bigl({\bf t}-\![a_{k}^{-1}]-\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{m-1}[b_{l}^{-1}]\Bigr)=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}d^{2}\zeta\bar{\rho}(\zeta)\,e^{\xi({\bf t},\zeta)}\frac{a_{k}-\zeta}{a_{k}}\Bigl(\prod_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}\!\!\frac{b_{l}-\zeta}{b_{l}}\Bigr)}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}\times\,\tau\Bigl({\bf t}\!-\![\zeta^{-1}]\!-\![a_{k}^{-1}]\!-\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{m-1}[b_{l}^{-1}]\Bigr)}.\end{array} (4.23)

Then the left-hand side of (4.21), call it FF, becomes, up to an irrelevant common factor:

F=∫ℂ∫ℂd2​z​d2​ζ​ρ^​(z)​ρ¯​(ζ)​eξ⁡(𝐭,z)+ξ⁡(𝐭,ζ)​(∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​(Rk​(z,ζ)+Rk​(ζ,z))),F=\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}\!\int_{\mbox{\Bbbb C}}d^{2}zd^{2}\zeta\hat{\rho}(z)\bar{\rho}(\zeta)\,e^{\xi({\bf t},z)+\xi({\bf t},\zeta)}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\Bigl(R_{k}(z,\zeta)+R_{k}(\zeta,z)\Bigr)\right),

where

Rk​(z,ζ)=Δm+1(a1,…,a^k,…,am+1,z)Δm+1(ak,b1,…,,bm−1,ζ)×τ⁡(𝐭−[z−1]−∑j=1,≠km+1[aj−1])​τ​(𝐭−[ζ−1]−[ak−1]−∑l=1m−1[bl−1]).\begin{array}[]{lll}R_{k}(z,\zeta)&=&\Delta_{m+1}(a_{1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{k},\ldots,a_{m+1},z)\Delta_{m+1}(a_{k},b_{1},\,\ldots,\,,b_{m-1},\zeta)\\ &&\\ &&\times\,\,\displaystyle{\tau\Bigl({\bf t}\!-\![z^{-1}]-\!\!\sum_{j=1,\neq k}^{m+1}[a_{j}^{-1}]\Bigr)\,\tau\Bigl({\bf t}\!-\![\zeta^{-1}]\!-\![a_{k}^{-1}]\!-\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{m-1}[b_{l}^{-1}]\Bigr).}\end{array} (4.24)

To unify the notation for the variables, denote z=am+2z=a_{m+2}, ζ=bm\zeta=b_{m}. Then, using the notation as in (2.10), we have:

Rk​(am+2,bm)=τ⁡[a1,…,am+2]​τ​[ak,b1,…,bm].R_{k}(a_{m+2},b_{m})=\tau\bigl[a_{1},\,\ldots,a_{m+2}\bigr]\,\tau\bigl[a_{k},b_{1},\,\ldots,b_{m}\bigr].

Then equation (2.10) with the change m→m+1m\to m+1 yields:

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​Rk​(am+2,bm)=(−1)m​τ​[a1,…,am+1]​τ​[am+2,b1,…,bm].\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}R_{k}(a_{m+2},b_{m})=(-1)^{m}\,\tau\bigl[a_{1},\ldots,a_{m+1}\bigr]\,\tau\bigl[a_{m+2},b_{1},\ldots,b_{m}\bigr]. (4.25)

Since the second multiplier is antisymmetric with respect to the interchange am+2↔bma_{m+2}\leftrightarrow b_{m}, we have

∑k=1m+1(−1)k−1​(Rk​(z,ζ)+Rk​(ζ,z))=0,\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{k-1}\Bigl(R_{k}(z,\zeta)+R_{k}(\zeta,z)\Bigr)=0,

so F=0F=0 and equation (4.20) is proved. By virtue of Proposition 4.2, this proves equation (4.19).  

Corollary 4.1

For all a,b∈ℂa,b\in\mbox{\Bbb C}, the function τ⁡(𝐭|a,b)=a​τ^​(𝐭)+b​τ¯​(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}|a,b)=a\hat{\tau}({\bf t})+b\bar{\tau}({\bf t}) is a tau-function of the KP hierarchy, i.e., it satisfies the integral bilinear relation (2.1). More generally, let nn pairs (τ,τ(α))(\tau,\tau^{(\alpha)}) (α=1,…,n\alpha=1,\ldots,n) be solutions to the mKP hierarchy, then for all c1,…,cn∈ℂc_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\in\mbox{\Bbb C} the function

τ⁡(𝐭|{c1,…,cn})=∑α=1ncα​τ(α)​(𝐭)\tau({\bf t}|\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\})=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}c_{\alpha}\tau^{(\alpha)}({\bf t})

is a KP tau-function.

This statement immediately follows from (4.19) and from the fact that all the τ(α)\tau^{(\alpha)}’s are KP tau-functions.

Corollary 4.2

Let (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}), (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) be any two solutions of the mKP hierarchy. Then the KP tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau}, τ¯\bar{\tau} satisfy the bilinear equation

a12​(τ^12​τ¯3+τ^3​τ¯12)+a23​(τ^23​τ¯1+τ^1​τ¯23)+a31​(τ^13​τ¯2+τ^2​τ¯13)=0,a_{12}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{12}\bar{\tau}^{3}+\hat{\tau}^{3}\bar{\tau}^{12}\Bigr)+a_{23}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{23}\bar{\tau}^{1}+\hat{\tau}^{1}\bar{\tau}^{23}\Bigr)+a_{31}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{13}\bar{\tau}^{2}+\hat{\tau}^{2}\bar{\tau}^{13}\Bigr)=0, (4.26)

where the short-hand notations (2.3) are used.

Proof. This is the simplest particular case of (4.20) obtained at m=2m=2, b1=∞b_{1}=\infty.  

Let us give another proof of equation (4.26) which is not based on explicit realization of the BD transformations. The starting point is the following system of equations of the type (3.7) written for the mKP solutions (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}) and (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}):

{a1​τ^13​τ23−a2​τ^23​τ13−a12​τ^3​τ123=0,a1​τ¯13​τ23−a2​τ¯23​τ13−a12​τ¯3​τ123=0,a2​τ^21​τ31−a3​τ^31​τ21−a23​τ^1​τ123=0,a2​τ¯21​τ31−a3​τ¯31​τ21−a23​τ¯1​τ123=0,a3​τ^32​τ12−a1​τ^12​τ32−a31​τ^2​τ123=0,a3​τ¯21​τ31−a1​τ¯12​τ32−a31​τ¯2​τ123=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}a_{1}\hat{\tau}^{13}\tau^{23}-a_{2}\hat{\tau}^{23}\tau^{13}-a_{12}\hat{\tau}^{3}\tau^{123}=0,\\ \\ a_{1}\bar{\tau}^{13}\tau^{23}-a_{2}\bar{\tau}^{23}\tau^{13}-a_{12}\bar{\tau}^{3}\tau^{123}=0,\\ \\ a_{2}\hat{\tau}^{21}\tau^{31}-a_{3}\hat{\tau}^{31}\tau^{21}-a_{23}\hat{\tau}^{1}\tau^{123}=0,\\ \\ a_{2}\bar{\tau}^{21}\tau^{31}-a_{3}\bar{\tau}^{31}\tau^{21}-a_{23}\bar{\tau}^{1}\tau^{123}=0,\\ \\ a_{3}\hat{\tau}^{32}\tau^{12}-a_{1}\hat{\tau}^{12}\tau^{32}-a_{31}\hat{\tau}^{2}\tau^{123}=0,\\ \\ a_{3}\bar{\tau}^{21}\tau^{31}-a_{1}\bar{\tau}^{12}\tau^{32}-a_{31}\bar{\tau}^{2}\tau^{123}=0.\end{array}\right.

Let us consider the first four equation. They form a system of homogeneous linear equations for τ12,τ23,τ31,τ123\tau^{12},\tau^{23},\tau^{31},\tau^{123}. Existence of nontrivial solutions implies that the matrix

M13=(0a1​τ^13−a2​τ^23−a12​τ^30a1​τ¯13−a2​τ¯23−a12​τ¯3−a3​τ^310a2​τ^21−a23​τ^1−a3​τ¯310a2​τ¯21−a23​τ¯1).M_{13}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}0&a_{1}\hat{\tau}^{13}&-a_{2}\hat{\tau}^{23}&-a_{12}\hat{\tau}^{3}\\ &&&\\ 0&a_{1}\bar{\tau}^{13}&-a_{2}\bar{\tau}^{23}&-a_{12}\bar{\tau}^{3}\\ &&&\\ -a_{3}\hat{\tau}^{31}&0&a_{2}\hat{\tau}^{21}&-a_{23}\hat{\tau}^{1}\\ \\ -a_{3}\bar{\tau}^{31}&0&a_{2}\bar{\tau}^{21}&-a_{23}\bar{\tau}^{1}\end{array}\right).

is degenerate, i.e., detM13=0\det M_{13}=0. Calculation of the determinant gives:

detM13a1​a2​a3=τ^13​τ¯13​R−(τ^13)2​H¯−(τ¯13)2​H^,\frac{\det M_{13}}{a_{1}a_{2}a_{3}}=\hat{\tau}^{13}\bar{\tau}^{13}R-(\hat{\tau}^{13})^{2}\bar{H}-(\bar{\tau}^{13})^{2}\hat{H},

where

R=a12​(τ^12​τ¯3+τ^3​τ¯12)+a23​(τ^23​τ¯1+τ^1​τ¯23)+a31​(τ^13​τ¯2+τ^2​τ¯13),H^=a12​τ^12​τ^3+a23​τ^23​τ^1+a31​τ^31​τ^2,H¯=a12​τ¯12​τ¯3+a23​τ¯23​τ¯1+a31​τ¯31​τ¯2.\begin{array}[]{l}R=a_{12}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{12}\bar{\tau}^{3}+\hat{\tau}^{3}\bar{\tau}^{12}\Bigr)+a_{23}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{23}\bar{\tau}^{1}+\hat{\tau}^{1}\bar{\tau}^{23}\Bigr)+a_{31}\Bigl(\hat{\tau}^{13}\bar{\tau}^{2}+\hat{\tau}^{2}\bar{\tau}^{13}\Bigr),\\ \\ \hat{H}=a_{12}\hat{\tau}^{12}\hat{\tau}^{3}+a_{23}\hat{\tau}^{23}\hat{\tau}^{1}+a_{31}\hat{\tau}^{31}\hat{\tau}^{2},\\ \\ \bar{H}=a_{12}\bar{\tau}^{12}\bar{\tau}^{3}+a_{23}\bar{\tau}^{23}\bar{\tau}^{1}+a_{31}\bar{\tau}^{31}\bar{\tau}^{2}.\end{array}

Since both τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau} are KP tau-functions, H¯=H^=0\bar{H}=\hat{H}=0 by virtue of equation (2.4). Therefore, detM13=0\det M_{13}=0 if and only if R=0R=0.

Remark 4.2

Equation (4.26) alone does not imply that τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau} are KP tau-functions. The simplest counterexample is τ^​(𝐭)=1\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=1 (satisfies KP), τ¯​(𝐭)=tn\bar{\tau}({\bf t})=t_{n} for n≥2n\geq 2 (does not satisfy KP), but this pair solves equation (4.26).

Corollary 4.3

The function

S⁡(𝐭)=τ¯​(𝐭)τ^​(𝐭)S({\bf t})=\frac{\bar{\tau}({\bf t})}{\hat{\tau}({\bf t})} (4.27)

satisfies the linear equation

a12​τ^3​τ^12​(S3+S12)+a23​τ^1​τ^23​(S1+S23)+a31​τ^2​τ^31​(S2+S31)=0,a_{12}\hat{\tau}^{3}\hat{\tau}^{12}(S^{3}+S^{12})+a_{23}\hat{\tau}^{1}\hat{\tau}^{23}(S^{1}+S^{23})+a_{31}\hat{\tau}^{2}\hat{\tau}^{31}(S^{2}+S^{31})=0, (4.28)

or, in a more compact form,

∑(α​β​γ)=(123)and​cyclesaα​β​τ^α​β​τ^γ​(Sα​β+Sγ)=0.\sum_{(\alpha\beta\gamma)=(123)\atop\rm and\;cycles}a_{\alpha\beta}\hat{\tau}^{\alpha\beta}\hat{\tau}^{\gamma}(S^{\alpha\beta}+S^{\gamma})=0. (4.29)

Proof. This directly follows from equation (4.26) after the substitution (4.27).  

There are more equations for the SS-function which follow from (4.26) just in an equally simple way as (4.29). An analog of (4.29) with the τ¯\bar{\tau}-function instead of τ^\hat{\tau} is

∑(α​β​γ)=(123)and​cyclesaα​β​τ¯α​β​τ¯γ​(1Sα​β+1Sγ)=0.\sum_{(\alpha\beta\gamma)=(123)\atop\rm and\;cycles}a_{\alpha\beta}\bar{\tau}^{\alpha\beta}\bar{\tau}^{\gamma}\Bigl(\frac{1}{S^{\alpha\beta}}+\frac{1}{S^{\gamma}}\Bigr)=0. (4.30)

From the fact that τ¯\bar{\tau} is a KP tau-function, it follows that along with (4.29) the function SS satisfies the bilinear equation

∑(α​β​γ)=(123)and​cyclesaα​β​τ^α​β​τ^γ​Sα​β​Sγ=0.\sum_{(\alpha\beta\gamma)=(123)\atop\rm and\;cycles}a_{\alpha\beta}\hat{\tau}^{\alpha\beta}\hat{\tau}^{\gamma}S^{\alpha\beta}S^{\gamma}=0. (4.31)
Theorem 4.3

The function S⁡(𝐭)S({\bf t}) defined in (4.27) satisfies the equation

S1−S12S3−S23⋅S2−S23S1−S13⋅S3−S13S2−S12=1,\frac{S^{1}-S^{12}}{S^{3}-S^{23}}\cdot\frac{S^{2}-S^{23}}{S^{1}-S^{13}}\cdot\frac{S^{3}-S^{13}}{S^{2}-S^{12}}=1, (4.32)

which is the discrete SchKP equation.

Theorem 4.4

Let ϕ⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t}), ϕ′​(𝐭)\phi^{\prime}({\bf t}) be two wave functions of the KP hierarchy associated with the KP tau-functions τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) and τ¯​(𝐭)\bar{\tau}({\bf t}) respectively. Then the following holds:

ℒ¯=S−1​ℒ​S.\bar{\cal L}=S^{-1}{\cal L}S. (4.42)

to be substituted into (4.45). After some simple transformations, equation (4.45) can be rewritten in the form

pk+1(−[∂x−1])φ+Wk∂xφ=0,k≥1.p_{k+1}(-[\partial_{x}^{-1}])\varphi+W_{k}\partial_{x}\varphi=0,\qquad k\geq 1. (4.53)

The structure of these equations allows one to express the derivative ∂tkφ\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi through derivatives ∂tlφ\partial_{t_{l}}\varphi with l<kl<k:

∂tkφ=𝖠k(∂tk−1,…,∂t1)φ,\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi={\sf A}_{k}(\partial_{t_{k-1}},\ldots,\partial_{t_{1}})\varphi,

where 𝖠k{\sf A}_{k} in the right-hand side is some differential operator in the variables t1,…,tk−1t_{1},\ldots,t_{k-1}. Applying it successively for k=2,3,…k=2,3,\ldots, it is possible to represent the right-hand side as a differential operator containing ∂t1=∂x\partial_{t_{1}}=\partial_{x} only:

∂tkφ=𝖡k(∂x)φ.\partial_{t_{k}}\varphi={\sf B}_{k}(\partial_{x})\varphi.

However, we already know from Corollary 3.1 that for the BA function the operators 𝖡k(∂x){\sf B}_{k}(\partial_{x}) coincide with the operators ℬk{\cal B}_{k} defined in (3.52) (see (3.58)). Since the function SS satisfies the same linear equations as the BA function φ\varphi, we conclude that from (4.51) it follows that ∂tkS=ℬk​S\partial_{t_{k}}S={\cal B}_{k}S, i.e., SS defined in (4.43) is indeed an mKP wave function.

It remains to prove the inverse statement: that any mKP wave function SS can be represented as a ratio of two KP tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau} obtained from some KP tau-function τ\tau as results of two forward BD transformations τ→τ^\tau\to\hat{\tau} and τ→τ¯\tau\to\bar{\tau}. This is already almost evident from the calculations done above. Indeed, we have checked that the BA function satisfies equation (4.52). Integrating it over zz with some density, we see that the same equation is satisfied by any wave function SS (i.e., equation (4.49)). But equation (4.48) means that SS can be represented as ratio of τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau}.  

Remark 4.3

The transformation τ^→τ¯\hat{\tau}\rightarrow\bar{\tau} is a BD transformation for KP hierarchy meaning that it sends any its solution to another solution. However, such BD transformations are in a sense of a different type than the forward and backward ones defined by equations (3.11) and (3.24) respectively. To be more precise, they can be realized as a composition of a forward and backward transformations, and for this reason they are called binary BD transformations. In this paper, we consider them from a slightly different angle than is usually accepted in the literature. Namely, following a more traditional approach one constructs a binary BD transformation starting from the pair (ϕ,ϕ′⁣∗)(\phi,\phi^{\prime*}) of a KP wave function and an adjoint one. In this approach, the role of the function SS (the function which satisfies the SchKP equation) is played by the Baker-Akhiezer kernel doubly integrated with two density functions (for details see, e.g., the recent review [33]). We, however, prefer to avoid dealing with adjoint wave functions and develop the theory using the couple of wave functions (ϕ,ϕ′)(\phi,\phi^{\prime}).

Now, let us prove an SchKP analogue of Theorem 3.3, i.e., the statement that is in a sense inverse to the one of Theorem 4.4.

Theorem 4.5

Let S⁡(𝐭)S({\bf t}) be any solution to the SchKP equation (4.32). Then there exist two functions τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}), τ¯​(𝐭)\bar{\tau}({\bf t}) such that:

  • a)

    The function SS is given by S​(𝐭)=τ¯​(𝐭)/τ^​(𝐭)S({\bf t})=\bar{\tau}({\bf t})/\hat{\tau}({\bf t});

  • b)

    Both τ^​(𝐭)\hat{\tau}({\bf t}) and τ¯​(𝐭)\bar{\tau}({\bf t}) are KP tau-functions satisfying the bilinear equation (2.1) and equation (4.26) that connects them.

Proof. The proof starts from rewriting equation (4.32) in the form

(S1−S12)​(S2−S23)​(S3−S13)=(S3−S23)​(S1−S13)​(S2−S12).(S^{1}-S^{12})(S^{2}-S^{23})(S^{3}-S^{13})=(S^{3}-S^{23})(S^{1}-S^{13})(S^{2}-S^{12}).

Note that it is invariant under cyclic permutation of indices (123)(123). Letting aγ→∞a_{\gamma}\to\infty for γ=1,2,3\gamma=1,2,3, we have:

Sxα​(Sβ−Sα​β)​(S−Sβ)=Sxβ​(Sα−Sα​β)​(S−Sα)S_{x}^{\alpha}(S^{\beta}-S^{\alpha\beta})(S-S^{\beta})=S_{x}^{\beta}(S^{\alpha}-S^{\alpha\beta})(S-S^{\alpha}) (4.54)

for (α​β)=(12),(23),(31)(\alpha\beta)=(12),(23),(31), where Sxα=∂xSαS_{x}^{\alpha}=\partial_{x}S^{\alpha}. In terms of the function

R⁡(𝐭,z)=S⁡(𝐭)−S⁡(𝐭−[z−1])Sx​(𝐭)R({\bf t},z)=\frac{S({\bf t})-S({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])}{S_{x}({\bf t})}

equation (4.54) acquires the form

R⁡(𝐭−[aα−1],aβ)R⁡(𝐭,aβ)=R⁡(𝐭−[aβ−1],aα)R⁡(𝐭,aα),\frac{R({\bf t}-[a_{\alpha}^{-1}],a_{\beta})}{R({\bf t},a_{\beta})}=\frac{R({\bf t}-[a_{\beta}^{-1}],a_{\alpha})}{R({\bf t},a_{\alpha})},

which allows us to apply Lemma 3.1. It then follows that there exists a function g⁡(𝐭)g({\bf t}) such that

R⁡(𝐭,a)=g⁡(𝐭−[a−1])a​g​(𝐭).R({\bf t},a)=\frac{g({\bf t}-[a^{-1}])}{a\,g({\bf t})}. (4.55)

A direct calculation (which uses equation (4.32)) shows that the function

ϕ⁡(𝐭)=1/g⁡(𝐭)\phi({\bf t})=1/g({\bf t}) (4.56)

satisfies equation (3.33), i.e., is a solution to the mKP hierarchy. Theorem 3.3 implies that there exists a pair of KP tau-functions τ,τ^\tau,\hat{\tau} connected by the bilinear equation (3.5) such that ϕ=τ^/τ\phi=\hat{\tau}/\tau.

Note that if SS is a solution to (4.32), then S′=S−1S^{\prime}=S^{-1} is another solution. Repeating the arguments above for this solution, we conclude that the function ϕ′=S​ϕ=S/g\phi^{\prime}=S\phi=S/g, as well as ϕ\phi, solves the mKP hierarchy. More generally, S′′=(a​S+b)/(c​S+d)S^{\prime\prime}=(aS+b)/(cS+d) for all a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mbox{\Bbb C} is a solution, too. In the same way, this implies that any linear combination ϕ′′=c​ϕ′+d​ϕ\phi^{\prime\prime}=c\phi^{\prime}+d\phi solves the mKP hierarchy. According to Proposition 3.2, ϕ\phi and ϕ′\phi^{\prime} (and ϕ′′\phi^{\prime\prime}) are wave functions corresponding to one and the same solution to KP with a tau-function τ\tau. Then ϕ=τ^/τ\phi=\hat{\tau}/\tau, ϕ′=τ¯/τ\phi^{\prime}=\bar{\tau}/\tau, and (τ,τ^)(\tau,\hat{\tau}), (τ,τ¯)(\tau,\bar{\tau}) are two solutions to the mKP hierarchy. Equations (4.19) and (4.28) that connect the tau-functions τ^,τ¯\hat{\tau},\,\bar{\tau} then follow from Theorem 4.2.  

Remark 4.4

It can be shown (see, e.g. [33]) that the pair of tau-functions (τ,τ¯^)(\tau,\hat{\bar{\tau}}) on the second diagonal in the square diagram (4.10) satisfy the integral bilinear relation

∮C∞z2​eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ¯^​(𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(𝐭′+[z−1])​𝑑z=0,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\oint_{C_{\infty}}z^{2}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime},z)}\hat{\bar{\tau}}({\bf t}-[z^{-1}])\tau({\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}])\,dz=0,}\end{array} (4.57)

and, therefore, can be regarded as a solution to the 2-mKP hierarchy in the sense of Section 3.1 (see (3.2)).

4.3 From mKP and SchKP to HD

We have shown that the bilinear formulation of the SchKP hierarchy requires two KP tau-functions τ^\hat{\tau} and τ¯\bar{\tau} such that they are connected by the bilinear equation (4.19). The dependent variable of the hierarchy is the SS-function, which is their ratio. The infinite hierarchy itself is obtained by expanding equation (4.32) in a Taylor series in negative powers of a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}.

A natural question arises whether the SchKP hierarchy admits a formulation of the Lax-Sato type, as it is the case for KP and mKP. In this section we show that the answer is yes, and the Lax-Sato form of the SchKP hierarchy is just what is called the (2+1) HD hierarchy.

First of all, we need some technical preparations. Let S⁡(x)S(x) and X⁡(s)X(s) be two mutually inverse functions: S∘X=X∘S=IdS\circ X=X\circ S=\mbox{Id}, or

S⁡(X⁡(s))=s,X⁡(S⁡(x))=x.S(X(s))=s,\qquad X(S(x))=x. (4.58)

Differentiating these formulas, we get

Sx​Xs=1,where​Sx≡∂xS⁡(x),Xs≡∂sX⁡(s),S_{x}\,X_{s}=1,\;\;\mbox{where}\;\;S_{x}\equiv\partial_{x}S(x),\;X_{s}\equiv\partial_{s}X(s),

where it is implied that xx and ss depend on each other as s=S⁡(x)s=S(x) (or x=X⁡(s)x=X(s)). Given any function f⁡(x)f(x) of xx, the corresponding function of ss is f⁡(X⁡(s))f(X(s)). The notation f(x)​(x)f^{(x)}(x) for the f⁡(x)f(x) and f(s)​(s)f^{(s)}(s) for f⁡(X⁡(s))f(X(s)) are sometimes useful, then we have the identity f(x)​(x)=f(s)​(s)f^{(x)}(x)=f^{(s)}(s) which states that the function ff is an invariant object defined regardless of the choice of coordinate (xx or ss). The vector fields ∂x\partial_{x} and ∂s\partial_{s} are connected by the formula

∂x=Sx∂s,Sx=Sx(X(s)).\partial_{x}=S_{x}\partial_{s},\quad S_{x}=S_{x}(X(s)). (4.59)

Consider pseudo-differential operators in the variables xx and ss:

A(x)=∑kak(x)(x)∂xk,A(s)=∑kak(s)(s)(Sx∂s)k,A^{(x)}=\sum_{k}a_{k}^{(x)}(x)\partial_{x}^{k},\qquad A^{(s)}=\sum_{k}a_{k}^{(s)}(s)(S_{x}\partial_{s})^{k}, (4.60)

with A(x)=A(s)A^{(x)}=A^{(s)} by the definition.

Lemma 4.2

For a pseudo-differential operaror A(x)=A(s)=AA^{(x)}=A^{(s)}=A it holds:

  • a)

    A≥1(s)=A≥1(x)A^{(s)}_{\geq 1}=A^{(x)}_{\geq 1},

  • b)

    A≥2(s)=A≥1(x)−(A≥1(x)S)Sx−1∂xA_{\geq 2}^{(s)}=A^{(x)}_{\geq 1}-(A^{(x)}_{\geq 1}S)S_{x}^{-1}\partial_{x},

    where (A≥1(x)​S)(A^{(x)}_{\geq 1}S) means action of the differential operator A≥1(x)A^{(x)}_{\geq 1} to the function S⁡(x)S(x).

The both equalities easily follow from the definitions. Some details of the proof can be found in [12].

The last technical remark is related to the case when the functions under consideration depend on a parameter tt (actually, we are interested in the case when the set of parameters 𝗍={t2,t3,t4,…}{\sf t}=\{t_{2},t_{3},t_{4},\ldots\} is infinite). Then the rule of change of variables from (x,t)(x,t) to (s,t)(s,t) implies that

∂t|x=∂t|s+St∂s,St≡∂tS(x,t),\partial_{t}\Bigr|_{x}=\partial_{t}\Bigr|_{s}+S_{t}\partial_{s},\quad S_{t}\equiv\partial_{t}S(x,t), (4.61)

where ∂t|x\partial_{t}\Bigr|_{x} (∂t|s\partial_{t}\Bigr|_{s}) is the partial derivative at constant xx (respectively, ss).

Now we are ready to reformulate the results of the previous section using the framework of pseudo-differential operators. Let S⁡(𝐭)=S⁡(x,𝗍)S({\bf t})=S(x,{\sf t}) (𝗍={t2,t3,…}{\sf t}=\{t_{2},t_{3},\ldots\}) be a wave function of the mKP hierarchy given by (4.43). In what follows it plays the role of the SS-function from (4.58) depending on the tkt_{k}’s as on parameters. So, we consider the change of variables x→sx\to s, where s=S⁡(x,𝗍)s=S(x,{\sf t}) (with fixed 𝗍{\sf t}). Consider the mKP Lax operator ℒ=ℒ(x){\cal L}={\cal L}^{(x)} (3.50) acting to functions of xx and its ss-version, as in (4.60):

ℒ(x)=∂x+∑k≥0vk(x)(x)∂x−k,𝖫(s)=Sx∂s+∑k≥0vk(s)(s)(Sx∂s)−k,{\cal L}^{(x)}=\partial_{x}+\sum_{k\geq 0}v_{k}^{(x)}(x)\partial_{x}^{-k},\qquad{\sf L}^{(s)}=S_{x}\partial_{s}+\sum_{k\geq 0}v_{k}^{(s)}(s)(S_{x}\partial_{s})^{-k}, (4.62)
Proposition 4.3

Let S⁡(x,𝗍)S(x,{\sf t}) be a wave function for the mKP Lax operator ℒ{\cal L} and the new independent space variable be s=S⁡(x,𝗍)s=S(x,{\sf t}). Then the Lax equations (3.64) for ℒ=ℒ(x){\cal L}={\cal L}^{(x)} imply the following Lax equations for 𝖫=𝖫(s){\sf L}={\sf L}^{(s)} given by (4.62):

∂tk𝖫=[(𝖫k)≥2,𝖫],k≥2\partial_{t_{k}}{\sf L}=[({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2},\,{\sf L}],\qquad k\geq 2 (4.63)

(the tkt_{k}-derivative in the left-hand side is taken at constant ss).

Proof. Using (4.61), we can write:

∂tk𝖫=[∂tk|s,𝖫]=[∂tk|x,ℒ]−[Stk∂s,𝖫]=∂tkℒ−[Stk∂s,𝖫].\partial_{t_{k}}{\sf L}=\Bigl[\partial_{t_{k}}\Bigr|_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr]=\Bigl[\partial_{t_{k}}\Bigr|_{x},\,{\cal L}\Bigr]-\Bigl[S_{t_{k}}\partial_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr]=\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal L}-\Bigl[S_{t_{k}}\partial_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr].

Next, using Lemma 4.2, we have:

∂tk𝖫−[(𝖫k)≥2,𝖫]=∂tkℒ−[Stk∂s,𝖫]−[(ℒk)≥1−((ℒk)≥1S)∂s,𝖫]\partial_{t_{k}}{\sf L}-[({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2},\,{\sf L}]=\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal L}-\Bigl[S_{t_{k}}\partial_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr]-\Bigl[({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}-(({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}S)\partial_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr]
=∂tkℒ−[(ℒk)≥1,𝖫]+[((ℒk)≥1S−Stk)∂s,𝖫].=\partial_{t_{k}}{\cal L}-\Bigl[({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1},\,{\sf L}\Bigr]+\Bigl[(({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}S-S_{t_{k}})\partial_{s},\,{\sf L}\Bigr].

If SS is a wave function for ℒ{\cal L}, i.e., Stk=(ℒk)≥1​SS_{t_{k}}=({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}S, then the last term in the right-hand side vanishes. The rest terms also vanish by virtue of the Lax equation for ℒ{\cal L}, and we obtain zero in the right-hand side. Therefore, the Lax equation (4.63) is proved.  

Comparing 𝖫{\sf L} with LHDL^{\rm HD} from (1.10), we see that to identify them one should put

U⁡(s,𝗍)=Sx​(X⁡(s),𝗍).U(s,{\sf t})=S_{x}(X(s),{\sf t}). (4.64)

In terms of the function UU we have:

∂x=U∂s.\partial_{x}=U\partial_{s}. (4.65)

So, 𝖫{\sf L} is the Lax operator for the HD hierarchy. Its dependent variable UU is directly connected with SS, the one subject to equations of the SchKP hierarchy. Namely, take the xx-derivative Sx​(x,𝗍)=∂xS⁡(x,𝗍)S_{x}(x,{\sf t})=\partial_{x}S(x,{\sf t}) and consider it as a function of ss (and of all the times) via the substitution x=X⁡(s,𝗍)x=X(s,{\sf t}), where X⁡(s,𝗍)X(s,{\sf t}) is the function inverse to S⁡(x,𝗍)S(x,{\sf t}), as equation (4.64) suggests.

The dressing operator 𝖶{\sf W} for the HD hierarchy is a pseudo-differential operator in the variable ss of the form

𝖶=w0+w1(U∂s)−1+w2(U∂s)−2+…{\sf W}=w_{0}+w_{1}(U\partial_{s})^{-1}+w_{2}(U\partial_{s})^{-2}+\ldots (4.66)

such that

𝖫=𝖶U∂s𝖶−1=U∂s+v0+v1(U∂s)−1+….{\sf L}={\sf W}\,U\partial_{s}{\sf W}^{-1}=U\partial_{s}+v_{0}+v_{1}(U\partial_{s})^{-1}+\ldots\,. (4.67)

In fact it is the mKP dressing operator 𝒲{\cal W} in which the change of variables x→sx\to s is done.

By analogy with Definition 3.1 it is natural to introduce wave functions for the HD hierarchy.

Definition 4.1

Any solution Φ⁡(s,𝗍)\Phi(s,{\sf t}) to the system of linear differential equations

∂tkΦ⁡(s,𝗍)=𝖡k​Φ​(s,𝗍),𝖡k=(𝖫k)≥2,k≥2\partial_{t_{k}}\Phi(s,{\sf t})={\sf B}_{k}\Phi(s,{\sf t}),\qquad{\sf B}_{k}=({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2},\quad k\geq 2 (4.68)

is called wave function for the HD Lax operator 𝖫{\sf L} (4.67).

Wave functions for the HD hierarchy admit a simple description in terms of those for the mKP hierarchy.

Proposition 4.4

Let S⁡(x,𝗍)S(x,{\sf t}) and S~​(x,𝗍)\tilde{S}(x,{\sf t}) be two wave functions of the mKP hierarchy. Then Φ⁡(s,𝗍)=S~​(X⁡(s,𝗍),𝗍)\Phi(s,{\sf t})=\tilde{S}(X(s,{\sf t}),{\sf t}) is a wave function of the HD hierarchy associated with SS (as before, X⁡(s,𝗍)X(s,{\sf t}) is the function inverse to S⁡(x,𝗍)S(x,{\sf t})). Moreover the opposite is also true: if Φ⁡(s,𝗍)\Phi(s,{\sf t}) is a wave function of the HD hierarchy associated with SS, then there exists a wave function S~​(s,𝗍)\tilde{S}(s,{\sf t}) of the mKP hierarchy such that Φ⁡(s,𝗍)=S~​(X⁡(s,𝗍),𝗍)\Phi(s,{\sf t})=\tilde{S}(X(s,{\sf t}),{\sf t}).

Proof. According to the definitions and Lemma 4.2 we can write the following chain of equalities:

∂tkΦ⁡(s,𝗍)−(𝖫k)≥2​Φ​(s,𝗍)=∂tkS~​(x,𝗍)+∂tkX⁡(s,𝗍)​S~x​(x,𝗍)−(𝖫k)≥2​S~​(X⁡(s,𝗍),𝗍)=OPEN(ℒk)≥1​S~−(ℒk)≥1​S~+(ℒk)≥1​S)​Sx−1​S~x+∂tkX⁡(s,𝗍)​S~x=(∂tkX⁡(s,𝗍)+∂tkS⁡(x,𝗍)​Sx−1​(x,𝗍))​S~x\begin{array}[]{lll}\partial_{t_{k}}\Phi(s,{\sf t})-({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2}\Phi(s,{\sf t})&=&\partial_{t_{k}}\tilde{S}(x,{\sf t})+\partial_{t_{k}}X(s,{\sf t})\tilde{S}_{x}(x,{\sf t})-({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2}\tilde{S}(X(s,{\sf t}),{\sf t})\\ &&\\ &=&({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}\tilde{S}-({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}\tilde{S}+({\cal L}^{k})_{\geq 1}S)S_{x}^{-1}\tilde{S}_{x}+\partial_{t_{k}}X(s,{\sf t})\tilde{S}_{x}\\ &&\\ &=&\Bigl(\partial_{t_{k}}X(s,{\sf t})+\partial_{t_{k}}S(x,{\sf t})S_{x}^{-1}(x,{\sf t})\Bigr)\tilde{S}_{x}\end{array} (4.69)

Taking the tkt_{k}-derivative of the identity X⁡(S⁡(x,𝗍),𝗍)=xX(S(x,{\sf t}),{\sf t})=x, we get:

∂tkX⁡(s,𝗍)+∂tkS⁡(x,𝗍)​∂sX⁡(s,𝗍)=0\partial_{t_{k}}X(s,{\sf t})+\partial_{t_{k}}S(x,{\sf t})\partial_{s}X(s,{\sf t})=0

But ∂sX⁡(s,𝗍)=Sx−1​(x,𝗍)\partial_{s}X(s,{\sf t})=S_{x}^{-1}(x,{\sf t}) as they are derivatives of the mutually inverse functions. Therefore, the expression in the last line in (4.69) vanishes and we have

∂tkΦ⁡(s,𝗍)−(𝖫k)≥2​Φ​(s,𝗍)=0,\partial_{t_{k}}\Phi(s,{\sf t})-({\sf L}^{k})_{\geq 2}\Phi(s,{\sf t})=0,

which just means that Φ⁡(s,𝗍)=S~​(X⁡(s,𝗍),𝗍)\Phi(s,{\sf t})=\tilde{S}(X(s,{\sf t}),{\sf t}) is a wave function of the HD hierarchy if and only if S~\tilde{S} is a wave function of the mKP hierarchy.  

Remark 4.5

Since the differential operators 𝖡k{\sf B}_{k} are divisible by ∂s2\partial_{s}^{2} from the right, it is evident that the simplest HD wave functions are Φ=1\Phi=1 and Φ=s\Phi=s. The corresponding second mKP wave functions S~\tilde{S} from Proposition 4.4 in these two cases are S~=1\tilde{S}=1 and S~=S\tilde{S}=S respectively.

4.4 Wave functions and BD transformations

For both KP and mKP hierarchies, their wave functions allow one to construct other solutions by means of BD transformations. In the KP case, this is part a) of Theorem 3.1, and there is only one such solution corresponding to a given wave function. In the mKP case, given an mKP wave function SS, there are three different solutions described by Theorem 4.1. All this is summarized by the square in Fig.1, which is a pictorial version of diagrams (4.10) or (4.12). In the figure, the vertices correspond to KP tau-functions, the directed edges correspond to mKP Lax operators and the face corresponds to the Lax operator 𝖫{\sf L} of the HD hierarchy.

A similar pattern holds for HD wave functions.

Proposition 4.5

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be an mKP Lax operator and S,FS,F be its two wave functions, ℒ′=S−1​ℒ​S\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=S^{-1}\mathcal{L}S, ℒ^=Sx−1​∂xℒ​∂−1Sx\hat{\mathcal{L}}=S^{-1}_{x}\partial_{x}\mathcal{L}\partial^{-1}S_{x}, ℒ¯=Sx−1​S2​∂xS−1​ℒ​S​∂x−1S−2​Sx\bar{\mathcal{L}}=S^{-1}_{x}S^{2}\partial_{x}S^{-1}\mathcal{L}S\partial_{x}^{-1}S^{-2}S_{x}, then

F′=F​S−1,F^=Fx​Sx−1,F¯=S2​(F/S)x​Sx−1\begin{array}[]{c}F^{\prime}=FS^{-1},\qquad\hat{F}=F_{x}S_{x}^{-1},\qquad\bar{F}=S^{2}(F/S)_{x}S_{x}^{-1}\end{array} (4.70)

are wave functions of ℒ′{\cal L}^{\prime}, ℒ^\hat{\cal L} and ℒ¯\bar{\cal L} respectively.

Proof. First of all, we note that all the three cases can be considered at once since F′=V⁡(F)F^{\prime}=V(F), where VV is a pseudo-differential operator such that ℒ′=V​ℒ​V−1\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=V\mathcal{L}V^{-1}. The same holds for F^\hat{F} and F¯\bar{F}. Moreover, for V​ℒ​V−1V\mathcal{L}V^{-1} to be an mKP Lax operator, the relation ∂tkV=((V​ℒ​V−1)k)>1​V−V​(ℒk)>1\partial_{t_{k}}V=((V\mathcal{L}V^{-1})^{k})_{>1}V-V(\mathcal{L}^{k})_{>1} must hold. Calculating ∂tk(V⁡(F))\partial_{t_{k}}(V(F)), one gets

∂tk(V⁡(F))=(((V​ℒ​V−1)k)>1​V−V​(ℒk)>1−V​(ℒk)>1)​(F)=((V​ℒ​V−1)k)>1​(V⁡(F)),\partial_{t_{k}}(V(F))=(((V\mathcal{L}V^{-1})^{k})_{>1}V-V(\mathcal{L}^{k})_{>1}-V(\mathcal{L}^{k})_{>1})(F)=((V\mathcal{L}V^{-1})^{k})_{>1}(V(F)), (4.71)

which completes the proof.  

To depict the HD Lax operator 𝖫\sf L with its wave function Φ\Phi, we need to add an extra dimension to Fig.1, see the cube in Fig.2. Here, too, each vertex corresponds to a solution of the KP hierarchy, and each edge equipped with arrow symbolizes a solution to the mKP hierarchy. The bottom face corresponds to 𝖫=𝖫⁡(τ^,τ¯){\sf L}={\sf L}(\hat{\tau},\bar{\tau}); the diagonal from τ^\hat{\tau} to τ~\tilde{\tau} on the front face corresponds to FF, which is another wave function for ℒ\mathcal{L}, connected to Φ\Phi as in Proposition 4.4. Using Proposition 4.5 we define F′F^{\prime}, F^\hat{F}, F¯\bar{F}, from which the HD Lax operators corresponding to the walls of the cube can be defined.

Let us define the Lax operator corresponding to the roof of the cube. Firstly, we obtain the mKP Lax operator corresponding to the upper edge of the front wall: ℒ~=Fx−1​F2​∂xF−1​ℒ​F​∂x−1F−2​Fx\tilde{\mathcal{L}}=F^{-1}_{x}F^{2}\partial_{x}F^{-1}\mathcal{L}F\partial_{x}^{-1}F^{-2}F_{x}, then, according to Proposition 4.5, F2​(S/F)x​Fx−1F^{2}(S/F)_{x}F_{x}^{-1} is its wave function, which allows us to construct the desired Lax operator. The results are summarized in the following list of equations:

Here the notation 𝒜(r)\mathcal{A}^{(r)} means the operator 𝒜{\cal A} acting on functions of the variable rr, which in the first line is ff, in the second line is r1r_{1}, etc. These variables are defined as follows: f=Inv⁡(F)f={\rm Inv}(F), r1=Inv⁡(F/S)r_{1}={\rm Inv}(F/S), r2=Inv⁡(Fx/Sx)r_{2}={\rm Inv}(F_{x}/S_{x}), r3=Inv⁡((F/S)x/(S−1)x)r_{3}={\rm Inv}((F/S)_{x}/(S^{-1})_{x}), r4=Inv⁡((S/F)x/(F−1)x)r_{4}={\rm Inv}((S/F)_{x}/(F^{-1})_{x}), where Inv{\rm Inv} means the inverse function: H⁡(Inv⁡(H⁡(x)))=xH({\rm Inv}(H(x)))=x.

Moreover, there are expressions for the tau-functions associated with vertices of the cube in terms of τ^,τ,S,F\hat{\tau},\tau,S,F:

τ¯^=Sx​τ^τ,τ¯=S​τ^,τ¯~=(F/S)x​S2​τ^2τ,τ^~=Fx​τ^τ,τ~=F​τ^,τ¯^~=(FxSx)x​(S−1)x​τ^τ2.\begin{array}[]{lll}\displaystyle{\hat{\bar{\tau}}=\frac{S_{x}\hat{\tau}}{\tau},}&\bar{\tau}=S\hat{\tau},&\displaystyle{\tilde{\bar{\tau}}=(F/S)_{x}\frac{S^{2}\hat{\tau}^{2}}{\tau}},\\ &&\\ \displaystyle{\tilde{\hat{\tau}}=\frac{F_{x}\hat{\tau}}{\tau}},&\tilde{\tau}=F\hat{\tau},&\displaystyle{\tilde{\hat{\bar{\tau}}}=\left(\frac{F_{x}}{S_{x}}\right)_{x}(S^{-1})_{x}\frac{\hat{\tau}}{\tau^{2}}}.\end{array} (4.73)
Remark 4.6

As it was already mentioned, there are two distinct choices of HD wave functions Φ=s\Phi=s and Φ=c\Phi=c, and their linear combinations lead to the P​S​L​(2)PSL(2)-action on SS and consequently on 𝖫{\sf L}. The S→S+cS\rightarrow S+c with constant cc does not affect 𝖫{\sf L}, however, S→S−1S\rightarrow S^{-1} leads to the transformation 𝖫(s)→(s−1​𝖫​s)(1/s){\sf L}^{(s)}\rightarrow(s^{-1}{\sf L}s)^{(1/s)}. This can be also interpreted as the connection of the HD Lax operator to the side of the face, and since each face is two-sided, this transformation corresponds to a flip.

Remark 4.7

One can try to construct other solutions of the HD hierarchy (for example, using ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}}) to define Lax operators corresponding to the walls of the cube. However, the result will be the same up to a flip (see the previous remark). This is due to the commutativity of the BD transformations for the KP hierarchy.

5 Embedding into multi-component KP hierarchy

In this section we will show that the SchKP hierarchy defined by the bilinear equation (4.19) admits an embedding into the multi-component KP hierarchy [39, 40, 41, 42]. In this hierarchy, independent variables are nn infinite sets of (in general complex) “times”

𝐭={𝐭1,𝐭2,…,𝐭n},𝐭α={tα,1,tα,2,tα,3,…},α=1,…,n{\bf t}=\{{\bf t}_{1},{\bf t}_{2},\ldots,{\bf t}_{n}\},\qquad{\bf t}_{\alpha}=\{t_{\alpha,1},t_{\alpha,2},t_{\alpha,3},\ldots\,\},\qquad\alpha=1,\ldots,n

and nn additional variables s1,…,sn∈ℤs_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\in\mbox{\Bbb Z} such that

∑α=1nsα=0.\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}s_{\alpha}=0. (5.1)

By 𝐬{\bf s} we denote the vector 𝐬={s1,…,sn}{\bf s}=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\} and by 𝐞α{\bf e}_{\alpha} the vector whose α\alpha’s component is 1 and all other components are 0. We will also use the following standard notation:

(𝐭±[z−1]γ)α​j=tα,j±δα​γ​z−jj,ξ⁡(𝐭α,z)=∑j≥1tα,j​zj.\left({\bf t}\pm[z^{-1}]_{\gamma}\right)_{\alpha j}=t_{\alpha,j}\pm\delta_{\alpha\gamma}\frac{z^{-j}}{j},\qquad\xi({\bf t}_{\alpha},z)=\sum_{j\geq 1}t_{\alpha,j}z^{j}. (5.2)

In the bilinear formalism, the dependent variable is the tau-function τ⁡(𝐬,𝐭)\tau({\bf s},{\bf t}). The hierarchy is defined as an infinite set of bilinear equations for the tau-function which are encoded in the basic bilinear relation [39, 42]

∑μ=1nϵα​μ​(𝐬)​ϵβ​μ​(𝐬′)​∮C∞d​z​zsμ−sμ′+δα​μ+δβ​μ−2​eξ⁡(𝐭μ−𝐭μ′,z)×τ⁡(𝐬+𝐞α−𝐞μ,𝐭−[z−1]μ)​τ​(𝐬′+𝐞μ−𝐞β,𝐭′+[z−1]μ)=0\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\sum_{\mu=1}^{n}\epsilon_{\alpha\mu}({\bf s})\epsilon_{\beta\mu}({\bf s}^{\prime})\oint_{C_{\infty}}\!dz\,z^{s_{\mu}-s_{\mu}^{\prime}+\delta_{\alpha\mu}+\delta_{\beta\mu}-2}e^{\xi({\bf t}_{\mu}-{\bf t}_{\mu}^{\prime},\,z)}}\\ \\ \displaystyle{\phantom{aaaaaaaaaa}\times\tau\left({\bf s}+{\bf e}_{\alpha}-{\bf e}_{\mu},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}]_{\mu}\right)\tau\left({\bf s}^{\prime}+{\bf e}_{\mu}-{\bf e}_{\beta},{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}]_{\mu}\right)=0}\end{array} (5.3)

valid for all 𝐭{\bf t}, 𝐭′{\bf t}^{\prime}, 𝐬{\bf s}, 𝐬′{\bf s}^{\prime} subject to the constraint (5.1)). In (5.3) e​p​s​i​l​o​nα​μ​(𝐬)epsilon_{\alpha\mu}({\bf s}) is a sign factor defined as

ϵα​μ​(𝐬)={(−1)sα+1+…+sμ,α<μ1,α=μ−(−1)sμ+1+…+sαα>μ.\epsilon_{\alpha\mu}({\bf s})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\hskip 8.5359pt(-1)^{s_{\alpha+1}+\ldots+s_{\mu}},&\quad\alpha<\mu\\ \hskip-42.67912pt1,&\quad\alpha=\mu\\ -(-1)^{s_{\mu+1}+\ldots+s_{\alpha}}&\quad\alpha>\mu.\end{array}\right. (5.4)

Different bilinear relations for the tau-function of the Hirota-Miwa type which follow from (5.3) for special choices of 𝐬−𝐬′{\bf s}-{\bf s}^{\prime} and 𝐭−𝐭′{\bf t}-{\bf t}^{\prime} are given in [42].

The following well known statement directly follows from the general equation (5.3).

Proposition 5.1

The tau-function τ⁡(𝐬,𝐭)\tau({\bf s},{\bf t}), regarded as a function of 𝐭α{\bf t}_{\alpha}, with any 𝐬{\bf s} and 𝐭μ{\bf t}_{\mu} with μ≠α\mu\neq\alpha fixed, is a tau-function of the KP hierarchy, i.e., it satisfies the bilinear equation (2.1).

 

Let us fix three distinct indices α,β,γ∈{1,2,…,n}\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\} such that α<β<γ\alpha<\beta<\gamma and consider the case when sμ=sμ′s_{\mu}=s^{\prime}_{\mu} unless μ=α,β,γ\mu=\alpha,\beta,\gamma and 𝐭μ=𝐭′μ{\bf t}_{\mu}={\bf t^{\prime}}_{\mu} unless μ=α\mu=\alpha (in the latter case we put 𝐭α=𝐭{\bf t}_{\alpha}={\bf t}, 𝐭′α=𝐭′{\bf t^{\prime}}_{\alpha}={\bf t^{\prime}} for simplicity of the notation). It is easy to see that in this case the sum in (5.3) contains only three non-zero terms:

∮C∞d​z​zsα−sα′​eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(𝐬,𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(𝐬′,𝐭′+[z−1])+ϵα​β(𝐬)ϵα​β(𝐬′)∮C∞dzzsβ−sβ′−2τ(𝐬+𝐞α−𝐞β,𝐭−[z−1]β)τ(𝐬′+𝐞β−𝐞β,𝐭′+[z−1]β)+ϵα​γ(𝐬)ϵα​γ(𝐬′)∮C∞dzzsγ−sγ′−2τ(𝐬+𝐞α−𝐞γ,𝐭−[z−1]γ)τ(𝐬′+𝐞β−𝐞γ,𝐭′+[z−1]γ)=0.\begin{array}[]{c}\displaystyle{\oint_{C_{\infty}}\!dz\,z^{s_{\alpha}-s_{\alpha}^{\prime}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}},\,z)}\tau\left({\bf s},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}]\right)\tau\left({\bf s}^{\prime},{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}]\right)}\\ \\ \displaystyle{+\,\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}({\bf s})\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}({\bf s^{\prime}})\oint_{C_{\infty}}\!dz\,z^{s_{\beta}-s^{\prime}_{\beta}-2}\tau\left({\bf s}+{\bf e}_{\alpha}-{\bf e}_{\beta},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}]_{\beta}\right)\tau\left({\bf s^{\prime}}+{\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\beta},{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}]_{\beta}\right)}\\ \\ \displaystyle{+\,\epsilon_{\alpha\gamma}({\bf s})\epsilon_{\alpha\gamma}({\bf s^{\prime}})\oint_{C_{\infty}}\!dz\,z^{s_{\gamma}-s^{\prime}_{\gamma}-2}\tau\left({\bf s}\!+\!{\bf e}_{\alpha}\!-\!{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}\!-\![z^{-1}]_{\gamma}\right)\tau\left({\bf s^{\prime}}\!+\!{\bf e}_{\beta}\!-\!{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}^{\prime}\!+\![z^{-1}]_{\gamma}\right)}=0.\end{array} (5.5)

Putting here 𝐬=𝐞β−𝐞γ{\bf s}={\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\gamma}, 𝐬′=𝟎{\bf s^{\prime}}={\bf 0} or 𝐬=𝟎{\bf s}={\bf 0}, 𝐬′=𝐞β−𝐞γ{\bf s^{\prime}}={\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\gamma}, we see that the last two integrals are given by residues at infinity. This leads to the following two equations:

12​π​i​∮C∞eξ⁡(𝐭−𝐭′,z)​τ​(𝐞β−𝐞γ,𝐭−[z−1])​τ​(𝟎,𝐭′+[z−1])​𝑑z+ϵα​β​(𝐞β−𝐞γ)​ϵα​β​(𝟎)​τ​(𝐞α−𝐞γ,𝐭)​τ​(𝐞β−𝐞α,𝐭)=0,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle{\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{C_{\infty}}e^{\xi({\bf t}-{\bf t^{\prime}},\,z)}\tau\left({\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}-[z^{-1}]\right)\tau\left({\bf 0},{\bf t}^{\prime}+[z^{-1}]\right)\,dz}\\ \\ \phantom{aaaaaaaaaaaaaa}+\displaystyle{\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}({\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\gamma})\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}({\bf 0})\tau\left({\bf e}_{\alpha}-{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}\right)\tau\left({\bf e}_{\beta}-{\bf e}_{\alpha},{\bf t}\right)=0},\end{array} (5.6)

It is easy to see that

Therefore, summing the two equations (5.6), (5.7), we obtain the equation

which coincides with (4.19) after the identification

τ⁡(𝟎,𝐭)=τ^​(𝐭),τ⁡(𝐞β−𝐞γ,𝐭)=τ¯​(𝐭).\tau\left({\bf 0},{\bf t}\right)=\hat{\tau}({\bf t}),\qquad\tau\left({\bf e}_{\beta}\!-\!{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}\right)=\bar{\tau}({\bf t}). (5.9)

It also follows from Proposition 5.1 that both τ⁡(𝟎,𝐭)\tau\left({\bf 0},{\bf t}\right) and τ⁡(𝐞β−𝐞γ,𝐭)\tau\left({\bf e}_{\beta}\!-\!{\bf e}_{\gamma},{\bf t}\right) are KP tau-functions.

Summarizing, in this section we have proved the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1

The SchKP hierarchy is embedded into the nn-component KP hierarchy with n≥3n\geq 3 in the following way. The independent variables corresponding to all but three components are to be frozen and put equal to zero (for definiteness, let the three unfrozen components be numbered by indexes 1, 2, 3 with the tau-function τ⁡(𝐬,𝐭)=τ⁡(s1,s2,s3,𝐭1,𝐭2,𝐭3)\tau({\bf s},{\bf t})=\tau(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3};{\bf t}_{1},{\bf t}_{2},{\bf t}_{3})). Then

τ^​(𝐭)=τ⁡(0,0,0,𝐭,𝟎,𝟎),τ¯​(𝐭)=τ⁡(0,1,−1,𝐭,𝟎,𝟎)\hat{\tau}({\bf t})=\tau(0,0,0;{\bf t},{\bf 0},{\bf 0}),\quad\bar{\tau}({\bf t})=\tau(0,1,-1;{\bf t},{\bf 0},{\bf 0})

is a pair of tau-functions for the SchKP hierarchy, i.e., they satisfy equation (4.19).

 

6 Concluding remarks

The main result of this paper is the established equivalence between the Harry Dym (HD) hierarchy of partial differential equations and the bilinear integral equation (4.19) for pairs (τ^,τ¯)(\hat{\tau},\bar{\tau}) of functions such that each of them is a tau-function of the KP hierarchy (i.e. satisfies (2.1)). More precisely, equation (4.19) defines the Schwarzian KP (SchKP) hierarchy within the framework of the bilinear formalism while the HD hierarchy arises as its equivalent reformulation in terms of the Lax-Sato approach. In contrast to what happens for the KP and mKP hierarchies, such reformulation requires switching to a new space variable s=S⁡(x)s=S(x), with SS being a wave function for the Lax operator of the mKP hierarchy, so ∂x=Sx∂s\partial_{x}=S_{x}\partial_{s}, and U⁡(s)U(s) from (1.9) and (1.10) (the dependent variable in the HD equation) is defined as U=SxU=S_{x}.

Another result is an embedding of the SchKP hierarchy into the multi-component KP hierarchy, which, to the best of our knowledge, was not discussed in the literature before. Also, some known results related to Bäcklund-Darboux transformations of integrable hierarchies have been reformulated in this paper in terms of tau-functions.

An interesting open question is whether the bilinear equation (4.26) (which was obtained as a particular corollary of the more general integral equation (4.19) is actually equivalent to the whole hierarchy, like this is the case for the KP and mKP hierarchies. The problem is that the direct method of proving this equivalence based on some determinant or pfaffian identities (suggested in [36] for KP, mKP and BKP) seems to be not applicable to (4.26) because of a more complicated structure of the equation. So, one should probably try to apply some indirect methods (similar to those developed in [35]). Another open question is whether any solution to SchKP can be realized as a solution to the multi-component KP hierarchy.

At last, we note that the connection with Bäcklund-Darboux transformations and integrable discretizations of soliton equations deserves further study. In particular, this seems to be an especially promising direction of further investigation, taking into account that BD transformations of integrable hierarchies play an important role in applications to quantum integrable model solvable by Bethe ansatz (see, e.g. the recent review [43]).
